The same distinction can apply to an extraordinary record if its actual rule provides a statement rather than a guaranteed true account. Ask what the method establishes and carry that forward honestly. A limited answer can still change who the party questions next.
The witness was facing another way

Change the example: the witness heard the repairer but did not see the gate. That observation may support a timeline while leaving the physical event unresolved. The party can compare sounds, damage, another account, or the repair records. Do not pretend the missing view exists because the witness looks authoritative. For an exercise, explain how one clue supports two different interpretations. A broken hinge might result from deliberate force or an overloaded mechanism. Name another piece of evidence that would distinguish them. The explanation demonstrates reasoning from actual information, not extracting a preferred conclusion from a sufficiently high result.
Sense a location, not a whole biography
**Original worked example.** SENSES AND TARGETS
The sound beneath the boards

A creature moves beyond a wall, and the party hears the floor creak. In this example, ordinary hearing gives a direction and a reason to be cautious; the table must decide whether it locates the particular target accurately enough for the proposed action. A granted contact sense may establish more, within its actual scope. Do not replace that reading with the creature’s name or an assumption that all unusual senses behave alike. Ask which surface is involved, what information reaches the character, and what remains uncertain.
Read the sense as a rule

Vision, blindsight, tremorsense, and other authored methods can provide legitimate target location. They differ in medium, reach, conditions, and the information they convey. Read the particular grant rather than borrowing a definition from another game. The hollowbark listener’s rooted posture is a useful picture of contact with a place, but the picture cannot extend a rule through every wall or floor. Exceptional perception should be explained in a sentence another player can use: what is sensed, where, and under what conditions.
Location is one part of targeting

Suppose a granted sense establishes that a person stands behind the partition. That answers the location question. The working still needs its actual subject, behavior, reach, and delivery method. A projected effect can meet the partition as an obstacle; a properly granted direct manifestation follows its own targeting terms. Neither method acquires mind reading because a location is known. Keep the separate questions visible. A permission to affect a known person is not permission to know their identity, intentions, equipment, or every condition they carry.
Ask what changed

The target climbs from the contacted floor onto a suspended platform. The party should reassess what the sense can establish now. A remembered location may be useful evidence, but it need not remain exact after movement. Another player can watch an exit, listen, illuminate the room, or negotiate access to the space. These ordinary contributions matter because perception is situated. Avoid treating the initial successful location as a permanent lock unless the acquired rule actually provides that continuing information. The scene may now support a different plan.
Give uncertainty a place

If the sense does not locate the target, propose a known area or spot where an action could reasonably be attempted. Explain what success would change and what the uncertainty means. An area does not guarantee a hidden person is inside it. The DM can resolve the unknown circumstance without granting invented knowledge to the character. Write the actual sensory condition beside the working on paper. When the target changes position or the medium disappears, everyone can recognize which question must be reopened.
A conversation about the contacted surface

Player: “My granted sense uses contact with the floor. Can it locate someone in this room?” DM: “Read the stated medium and reach. The person on the landing is connected through the stone; the suspended platform presents another question.” Player: “Then I can target the located person with a suitable working, but I do not claim a location on the platform.” The table applies the actual grant rather than accepting or rejecting every contact sense as one package. The player can now ask a companion to observe the platform. Different methods provide complementary information without silently giving all characters the same exceptional perception.
The exercise: say what the sense cannot reveal

Choose one acquired sense and write a successful observation in plain language. Then identify something that observation does not establish: a motive, a private name, the contents of a sealed bag, or an unrelated event elsewhere. Explain the difference using the actual rule. A target location can be enough for a particular working without supplying a complete biography. Now change the medium or position and review the sense again. If your example assumes the answer survives every change, check whether the grant truly says so. A strong sensory permission has meaningful scope; it does not need to answer every possible question to be useful.
A hidden creature still needs a location
**Original worked example.** CONCEALMENT WORKSHOP
A trail is not a target

In this example, a silent cat has crossed a ruined observatory. The party finds disturbed dust and a strand of fur near a broken window. Those clues establish a passage, not a guaranteed present location. A player can follow the signs, watch the exits, or ask what cover interrupts the view. The DM need not hide every visible fact behind a check. Useful description gives players places to investigate. Keep the distinction between evidence of past movement and perception of the creature now.
Make the search understandable

“I look for the creature” becomes clearer when the player names a position and method. From the doorway, can they see under the desk? Will moving the lantern illuminate the balcony or reveal the searcher? Does a companion cover the stair? The table can appraise uncertainty and consequences from those details. Concealment does not always mean a special rule called invisibility, and an unusual appearance does not establish either. Read the creature’s actual abilities if an exceptional concealment effect matters to the scene.
Preserve what the clue gives you

A fresh sound comes from the upper landing. It might locate a creature sufficiently for a particular attempt, or it might leave only a likely region. Establish that before committing. A player may have an applicable sense that changes the answer, while another only has ordinary hearing. The group can share observations without granting each observer the same sense. Describing what you noticed lets companions choose their own legitimate methods. Information can make cooperation easier without becoming an automatic shared targeting permission.
Aim at a known place when appropriate

The player chooses to disturb the visible curtain rather than claim a precise unseen target behind it. This is an attempt at a known object or area. It still needs the actual working’s access and scope. The curtain may move while the creature has already left, or it may reveal someone who was there. State what the effect does to that place, not what you hope it proves. The scene’s result can provide new information, but wishing for a hidden recipient does not put one inside the area.
Use the result, including a quiet result

The party finds a safe route to the balcony and discovers the cat guarding an injured companion. Their next choice can be to withdraw, offer space, investigate the injury, or risk a closer approach. Successful searching need not end in attack. If nothing is found, the party still knows which places it checked and what precautions it took. Record those facts. Repeating an identical search endlessly should not replace deciding whether to widen the search, wait, or pursue a different objective.
A conversation beside the curtain

Player: “I think the cat is behind the curtain, so I target it there.” DM: “You have evidence it went that way, but no current location. Can your method affect the known curtain or area?” Player: “I can disturb the curtain itself. That may reveal what is there.” Companion: “I watch the side passage while you do.” The group now has a clear method and a way to use any new information. It has not assumed that the hidden creature stayed put. If the curtain moves and nothing is visible, the watched exit and earlier clues still matter to the next decision.
The exercise: three different kinds of confidence

Compare seeing a creature at a window, finding fresh prints near that window, and knowing that the creature usually sleeps there. The first can establish a current sensory location if the relevant conditions permit. The second is evidence of movement. The third is prior information about a habit. Neither of the latter automatically supplies a present targeting lock. Describe a useful action from each situation. Observing a known opening, following a trail, or questioning someone about the habit can all move the scene forward. The answer should preserve what is genuinely known while giving the character an intelligible way to act.
A known target still needs a route
**Original worked example.** DELIVERY AND OBSTACLES
Four questions at the doorway

A surveyor stands across a cluttered chamber. You can see it through a narrow gap. In this example, begin with four questions: can you locate the particular target, does your acquired rule permit the intended change, does the reach cover it, and can this delivery method operate through the situation? A clear yes to sight is useful. It does not settle the other questions. Keep an obstacle in the description long enough for its practical effect to be appraised instead of letting a dramatic ability name erase it.
Follow the projected path

A projected working travels along an actual delivery path. Pillars, screens, people, and openings can therefore matter. The table applies the relevant authored scope and cover treatment to the proposed path. A player can seek a different angle, remove an obstacle, or ask a companion to change the scene. Do not assume that acquiring a larger range bypasses the obstruction. Range permits reach; it does not turn a projected delivery into direct manifestation or make an unknown recipient visible through everything between you.
Read direct manifestation carefully

A properly granted direct manifestation does not use projected cover penalties merely because an object lies between actor and target. It still needs a legitimate targeting method and the actual permission to produce its result. “I do it directly” cannot rewrite a working whose delivery was acquired differently. Ask where the effect begins, what it changes, and how that recipient is identified. An authored exception can be exciting, but its source and limits must be available to the table before someone relies on it.
Changing position is real work

The player moves toward a second opening while another holds the surveyor’s attention. Track the actor’s remaining movement across the whole round. Arriving at a new phase does not refill it. If the proposed move exceeds the remaining allowance, use an appropriate acquired extension or agree a contextual consequence before committing. The new angle may improve the path while exposing the mover. That is a meaningful tactical decision because both parts of the scene remain true. Movement should change circumstances, not merely repaint an attack bonus.
Describe the final attempt

“From this opening, I can see the surveyor’s frame and project the working through the clear gap” is a playable description. Resolve whatever meaningful uncertainty remains with the established check, defense, or agreed method. If the target moves or the screen falls, reassess the relevant part of the plan. On paper, a quick sketch of actor, obstacle, opening, and recipient is often enough. It records the shared geometry without requiring a precise tactical map for every discussion or importing another game’s cover rules.
A conversation about the gap

Player: “I can see the frame through the opening. My effect is projected.” DM: “Show the path from your position. The screen covers most of that line.” Player: “I move toward the second opening, using what movement remains.” Companion: “I can warn you if the surveyor turns.” The table can now appraise the actual path and any meaningful interference. This example does not guarantee that the new angle is clear or that watching grants a mechanical bonus. It keeps each contribution specific. If the player instead has a direct manifestation, read that method honestly rather than relabeling the projected effect after encountering an inconvenient screen.
The exercise: four answers on one sketch

Draw an actor, a located recipient, and a wall between them. Write the acquired behavior, reach, and delivery beside the drawing. Can you explain the attempt without assuming that one answer settles all the others? A visible recipient can still lie outside reach. A recipient within reach can remain unknown. A located target can be blocked from a projected trajectory while an actual direct manifestation uses different delivery terms. The sketch is successful when those distinctions are clear. It need not import precise grid movement or another game’s cover categories to make the party’s proposed method understandable.
An area is a real place
**Original worked example.** RECIPIENTS AND SELECTIVITY
Name what occupies the space

A damaged landing holds a worker, a rescuer, a broken stair, and loose boards. In this example, the player wants to influence an area around them. Describe the actual place before resolving the working. Which parts are inside its acquired shape? Which subjects can the rule affect? Where do its effects originate? A named area is not an abstract pile of enemies. Its contents can include companions, objects, bystanders, and empty space, each of which matters according to the actual rule.
An area does not invent a behavior

A player who can move existing water may arrange water through a permitted area. That permission does not automatically heal everyone within it, extinguish every kind of hazard, or distinguish friends by loyalty. Those outcomes require their actual subject and behavior. Output, reach, shape, duration, and selectivity describe different parts of an expression. Read the ingredients that establish each needed part. A larger delivery can distribute an eligible result; it cannot manufacture a missing verb or convert a harmful effect into a beneficial one.
Ask who is meant to be affected

The player wants to clear water around the stranded worker while leaving the support under the rescuer intact. The table examines whether this arrangement fits the actual working. If selective control is not available, a less ambitious route may solve the problem: guide a smaller flow, move the rescuer first, or use tools around the support. State the desired exclusions before commitment. A friendly character should not be secretly exempted after resolution just because the effect’s name sounded protective. The record and agreed expression determine the recipients.
Keep each effect legible

A capability may contain several effects, but nesting them does not silently give each a free independent action or an unrelated recipient. Explain how the declared working coheres and what each part changes. A real use may need more information than its short title. The party can still make an elegant combined plan; elegance comes from understandable dependencies. If two parts need different subjects or targeting methods, show them. If a condition ends one part, do not assume that all other consequences also disappear unless their rules say so.
Learn from the changed space

The player chooses to drain the landing before anyone crosses. The revealed boards show that another support is broken. This new information changes the rescue route. Alternatively, an attempted flow can leave a slippery surface or move debris toward the bank under the agreed consequences. Record the actual scene rather than only a success label. When an area working ends, ask what was temporary, what physically changed, and what still needs cleanup. The distinction makes later choices understandable without introducing a universal automatic aftermath rule.
A conversation about the exclusion

Player: “I want the flow to move the debris, but not the rescuer.” DM: “Which part of your actual rule provides that arrangement?” Player: “It controls existing water; it does not directly move every subject in the area. I will guide the flow away from the rope instead.” Companion: “Then I keep the worker on the dry section.” The proposed selectivity has become a concrete route rather than an automatic exemption for friends. The table still appraises the actual volume, obstacles, and risk. The example illustrates asking which part of the effect can genuinely be shaped, not requiring every area working to be hazardous.
The exercise: recipients before results

Sketch a small space with a companion, a bystander, an object, and the intended target. Select a working your character actually owns and state what it would change in that space. Which recipients are covered by its subject and arrangement? Which are excluded by an actual rule or practical route? Do not answer only “enemies.” Explain how the effect identifies them, if it really does. Now move the bystander and ask whether the attempt must change. The exercise teaches you to preserve the working’s actual recipients while discussing a vivid scene, rather than adding invisible exclusions after resolution because the outcome became awkward.
Negotiate the consequence you mean
**Original worked example.** COST CONVERSATION
Make an offer the table can examine

In this example, a water shaper wants to hold a damaged crossing while companions evacuate a worker. Say what happens, how long help is needed, and what pressure makes the attempt demanding. The DM and player can discuss an execution consequence before the attempt is committed. It might involve Vitality, continued direction, lost access until an agreed condition, a task, or a narrative complication. Do not assume that every extraordinary use owes the same kind of payment. The interesting choice begins with understanding what is at stake.
Separate purchase from execution

The character already acquired the ingredients. Their BU prices describe that acquisition and were reviewed for the campaign. Execution Cost describes this use in this situation. It is not a new purchase of every nested ingredient. Conversely, offering a larger execution payment does not automatically acquire an unrelated new permission. If the player needs a different behavior, identify it honestly. The table can review a new authored ingredient or agree a clear contextual exception, rather than hiding an expanded power inside a vague promise to pay more.
Compare two possible burdens

The player offers to remain at the bank directing the support until everyone crosses. A companion worries that this will prevent the shaper from rescuing someone upstream. The alternative offer is a more forceful expression with a different agreed consequence. These are example negotiations, not fixed prices. Ask which option preserves the desired scene and gives the player a meaningful choice. A restriction should specify what is restricted, when it applies, and how it ends. A narrative complication should have a comprehensible relationship to the attempt.
Agree what persistence requires

If the working is maintained, record its continuation terms and the agreed maintenance point. Council is a useful shared point in the round rhythm. One capability’s multiple effects do not automatically become several independent upkeep tracks, while several maintained capabilities carry their respective agreed requirements. Damage-triggered additional repayment for Vitality-only upkeep remains an unresolved alpha question. Do not fill that gap with an automatic counter policy. The table can use clearly agreed continuation consequences without pretending that the pending numerical scheme is settled.
Respect the chosen outcome

After agreement, resolve the attempt and apply its actual result. If the player accepts a temporary loss of access, a new round does not erase it unless that was the stated ending condition. If the scene no longer needs the working, decide whether ending it avoids future maintenance and which established consequences remain. Write a brief record in plain words. The best negotiated consequence is one the player remembers and the table can administer, rather than an impressive paragraph that nobody can explain when the next choice arrives.
A conversation about an unwanted payment

DM: “Holding the channel under this pressure would require a continuing restriction.” Player: “I do not want to lose the working for the rest of the journey. Could I remain directing it until the crossing ends instead?” DM: “That fits this proposal if you stay in position.” Companion: “I can take the worker while you hold the route.” This is a negotiated example, not a formula for exchangeable prices. The player has identified which consequence they do not want and proposed a method that changes the pressure. The table can accept, revise, or explain why it does not fit. A meaningful offer makes the intended commitment visible before the action is resolved.
A second scene needs a second appraisal

Compare the same working used to move water between bowls in a calm workshop. The rescue’s urgency, people, and failing support are absent. Its exact consequence need not automatically follow every trivial use forever. Conversely, a more dangerous crossing does not guarantee the calm result simply because the capability is unchanged. Read any actual fixed cost in the rule, then appraise the contextual terms honestly. For an exercise, name one changed circumstance that would matter and explain why. More time, better support, a different recipient, or reduced scope can change the proposal without providing an unrelated new permission.
Keep one thing going
**Original worked example.** CONTINUING WORKINGS
The promise after the first moment

In this example, a character keeps water away from a camp beneath a leaking ledge. The initial success is only part of the useful result. Everyone needs to know whether the working continues by itself, requires the character’s direction, has an authored duration, or depends on an ongoing consequence. These possibilities are different. A water channel dug with ordinary tools can remain after the digger walks away; a maintained arrangement may not. Describe the actual method before treating all continuing results as one universal form of concentration. A capability’s record gives the conversation its starting point.
One coherent record

Write the capability, the active result, its recipient or place, the next maintenance point, and the condition that ends it. Several effects inside the capability should remain legible, but they do not automatically become separate upkeep tracks simply because the record has several headings. Another maintained capability has its own agreed continuation requirements. The party needs to recognize which working they are relying on. If someone says “the shelter is protected,” ask whether that means water diverted, heat retained, a barrier held, or several actual results. A single appealing name can otherwise conceal missing terms.
A conversation at Council

Player: “I keep the flow outside our bedding while we prepare to move.” DM: “Your agreed continuation requires directing it at Council. Will you maintain it this round?” Player: “Yes. I stay beside the channel. Can someone carry my pack?” Companion: “I will, while I check the route.” This example uses terms the table already accepted; it does not establish a universal payment. The decision gives the other characters a concrete contribution. Council makes continuation visible before new intents depend on it, rather than leaving a silent assumption buried in yesterday’s description of the capability.
Do not confuse ending with undoing

When the character ends the flow, temporary control stops according to its rule. The wet ground, displaced debris, and channel already dug remain whatever the actual scene establishes. An accepted exhaustion, lost access, or other consequence uses its own ending condition; it does not vanish because the capability is no longer active. Likewise, a persistent independent result need not demand upkeep simply because it lasts. Separate the working, its physical aftermath, and the actor’s consequences. This is especially helpful when another character wants to take over an ordinary task instead of inheriting an extraordinary permission.
The ledge breaks

Compare a changed situation. The first camp has a narrow leak; the second suffers a collapse that sends a new stream through the shelter. The existing record has not automatically expanded to solve the new problem. Ask whether its subject, scale, place, and control still cover the proposed result. The character can maintain the original protection while companions evacuate, attempt an eligible stronger expression with newly agreed consequences, or end it and choose another method. Damage alone does not invoke a settled universal Vitality repayment policy: that alpha detail remains pending. The changed situation demands a described choice.
A paper test before the next scene

Cover the capability’s prose and read only your continuation note. Can another player tell what remains active, what you must do next, and when they should stop relying on it? If the note says only “upkeep,” it is incomplete. Rewrite it in ordinary words using the actual agreement. Now imagine the actor moves, rests, becomes unable to act, or chooses another intent. Read the relevant rule for each condition rather than inventing the same answer for all four. A compact record succeeds when it preserves the specific continuing promise with little effort at the table.
Choose what deserves a reminder

A useful continuation reminder names the next decision, not every sentence of the capability. “At Council, decide whether to keep directing the channel from this position” tells the player what to do. “Active” alone does not. If the continuing term is a resource requirement, record the real resource and timing. If it is an obligation, record its completion condition. Compare these notes with the actual rule before the next scene. The reminder should shorten the conversation while preserving the specific requirement; it must not turn distinct forms of upkeep into one invented universal bill.
Help changes the problem
**Original worked example.** PARTY COOPERATION
An objective with several useful edges

A loading machine holds a failing freight platform above a group of workers. In this example, the party wants everyone clear before the support gives way. One person can warn the workers, another secure a line, another inspect the load, and another negotiate with the machine. These are distinct contributions toward the same outcome. The group need not make four identical attacks, and the DM need not invent a universal help bonus. Start by finding what each contribution actually changes. A character with little relevant extraordinary access may still see a route that the others have overlooked.
Ask the other player what helps

Offering assistance is easier when it leaves the actor a meaningful choice. Say, “Would a secured rope make your crossing possible?” or “If I talk to the keeper, can you check the support?” The answer might reveal that something else is more urgent. Do not narrate a companion’s acceptance, feeling, or success without their participation. A shared plan becomes clear when each person states their own contribution and the table understands its relationship to the objective. The group’s colorful abilities can coexist with practical observations, trust, and ordinary equipment.
A conversation beneath the platform

Player: “I want to bring the workers out, but I cannot hold the whole load.” Companion: “I can guide them along the clear wall. What keeps the passage open?” Third player: “I will ask the machine to lower the freight toward the empty bay.” DM: “It needs a safe destination. Show me the route you are offering.” The party now has questions to answer rather than a blanket promise of assistance. This example does not guarantee the machine’s cooperation. Its actual understanding, obligations, circumstances, and the party’s method determine how the conversation can be resolved.
A shared goal is not shared permission

The characters can share information, positions, and timing while retaining their own acquired rules. A companion’s ability to locate someone through a wall does not automatically grant that sense to every other actor. Carrying a character’s item does not necessarily confer its active benefits without the actual equipment conditions. Read what the proposed cooperation relies on. When a contribution makes a previously difficult task secure, the DM can acknowledge that changed situation. When uncertainty remains, resolve it intelligibly. Neither outcome needs a compulsory series of identical help checks.
When one part fails

Suppose the machine cannot lower the load because the bay is occupied. The evacuation route may still be useful. The line may still protect a worker who slips. The party can clear the bay, choose another destination, or change the goal to buying time. Do not erase successful contributions because the first complete plan failed. Conversely, do not claim that the completed warning also guarantees every worker escaped. Apply the actual result of each contribution. Shared objectives become more interesting when the group can see which parts worked and which changed the next decision.
The quiet character has something to do

Try this exercise: remove the party’s strongest extraordinary working from the example. List three useful contributions that remain. Suitable answers might include identifying the empty bay, moving bystanders, securing a line, calling a foreman, or keeping an exit clear. Their usefulness depends on the described site. Now restore the working and ask how those contributions support it. The lesson is not that everyone must perform a special role. A cooperative party offers opportunities to participate, including observation, planning, and conversation, without making a shy player compete for the most dramatic ability name.
Compare protection and persuasion

If the machine refuses to lower the load, a character guarding the exit can still protect workers while another seeks the keeper. If the keeper approves the change, the physical route must still be usable. Neither contribution automatically solves the other. Explain the relationship between them in a short sentence: “Your agreement lets us try lowering it; my cleared passage lets people move when it lowers.” This is a practical way to review a shared plan. It rewards different approaches without forcing the party to pretend that every useful action grants the same numerical assistance.
Plan before the collision
**Original worked example.** AN ANNOTATED ROUND
The scene before Council

A rooftop challenger stands between the party and a banner that identifies a stolen shipment. In this worked example, the party wants the banner and a safe way down; defeating the challenger is one possible means. Describe the roof, its exits, loose tiles, and the challenger’s demands. Establish who can perceive whom and which extraordinary rules matter. The group should understand the objective before declaring intents. This avoids a familiar mistake: everyone starts attacking, and only later discovers that an ordinary negotiation or a different route could have served the original purpose.
Council makes promises visible

At Council, one player proposes distracting the challenger with a wager while another retrieves the banner and a third checks the descent. Discuss actual dependencies and likely consequences. Each character declares one coherent Main Intent; a longer description does not purchase several unrelated actions. Complexity comes from the work and dependencies of the attempt, not simply from how impressive it sounds. The table appraises the relevant Fast, Measured, or Heavy track. These example declarations do not establish fixed phase assignments for every conversation, climb, or extraordinary ability.
Fast is not a fresh turn

In this example’s agreed appraisal, the first direct exchange and preparatory movement happen in Fast. The challenger answers the wager, revealing that someone else has paid for the banner’s return. The information can affect later choices. Track any movement already spent against the character’s allowance for the entire round. Fast does not provide a new independent allowance or erase a continuing consequence. Nor must every participant manufacture a separate Fast action. A character whose intent depends on later work remains part of the shared scene while earlier results establish what happens next.
Measured and Heavy follow the situation

The banner retriever’s attempt resolves in Measured under the table’s appraisal, while the more involved work securing a descent resolves in Heavy. If the earlier exchange persuaded the challenger to permit retrieval, the Measured situation differs from the one first feared. If the challenger cuts off the route, the group must acknowledge that interference instead of completing a script unchanged. Apply the actual agreed resolution to each attempt. Tracks organize dependencies and shared timing; they are not a promise that every declared outcome occurs regardless of the scene around it.
A conversation when the plan changes

DM: “The challenger offers the banner if you recover the cargo from below.” Player: “My intent was to distract them while we took it. Can I accept instead?” Companion: “I can still finish the line; we may need it for the cargo.” The table can clarify the revised situation and commitments. This does not establish a universal free-intent replacement rule. It shows why declarations should be understandable enough to discuss interference and changed agreements. Do not treat improvisation as secretly obtaining several additional actions, or treat a reasonable clarification as grounds to ignore the fiction.
What the next Council needs

After Heavy, record where everyone is, which intents resolved, remaining consequences, active workings, and the banner’s actual status. Begin the next Council from that result. Reaction availability and round movement follow their proper refresh timing; lasting restrictions keep their stated conditions. A short recap can be spoken: “We have the banner, the challenger wants help, and the descent line is ready.” If the party did not secure the banner, say that just as clearly. The rhythm becomes useful when it carries a changed situation forward, without requiring initiative rolls or four separate personal turns per character.
The exercise: one intent through the rhythm

Write one objective for the rooftop scene, then describe the dependencies needed to pursue it. Ask the table to appraise their placement in the rhythm. Do not fill four boxes with four unrelated actions merely because there are four named phases. In the example, retrieving the banner can depend on a permitted approach and a safe route away; those details help explain timing and interference. The answer should preserve the coherent goal while showing what an earlier result can change. If your description contains another independent objective, identify it openly rather than hiding it as a decorative clause.
Spend the reaction on an opportunity
**Original worked example.** REACTIVE PLAY
An interruption you can describe

A companion’s foothold breaks above a canal. In this example, another character wants to respond before the fall carries them out of reach. A reaction begins with a perceived opportunity or threat and an intelligible immediate response. “I react” alone does not explain the attempt. Say what the actor notices, what they do, and which actual method makes it possible. The winged medic in the illustration evokes a rescue, but its presence is not a general permission for every character to fly, stop a fall, or heal someone at a distance.
The slot is not the ability

A character’s independent Reaction Slot permits reactive participation under the rhythm. It does not supply the ingredients of an extraordinary result. Grabbing an available line, warning someone, and producing a special descent effect rely on different circumstances or permissions. Read the actual working and its immediate scope. A reaction also needs to fit the event the actor can perceive. Knowing afterwards that a companion fell is different from being positioned and aware enough to intervene. Establish those details before resolving success instead of turning the slot into an unlimited exception to every access rule.
A short table exchange

Player: “I see the tile break. I throw the end of the rope I am holding.” DM: “The line can reach that position. You are trying to give them something to catch before they fall past it.” Companion: “I reach for it.” The table now has a concrete shared attempt and can resolve meaningful uncertainty. A different player might propose an acquired descent working with its own scope and consequences. These are alternative methods, not two automatic successes. The receiving character’s actual position and capacity remain part of the scene rather than a guarantee hidden inside the rescue’s name.
Keep the rest of the round honest

Mark the Reaction Slot when it is spent. It refreshes at Council, not whenever another dramatic event occurs or a new track begins. Movement used in the reaction still belongs to the round’s ordinary movement allowance unless an actual rule provides otherwise. A declared Main Intent and a reactive opportunity can interact; appraise their real dependencies and interference at the table. Do not quietly finish an impossible earlier plan merely because its card remains on the sheet. Reacting can create a useful tradeoff without demanding an invented universal cancellation rule.
Now the actor cannot see the fall

Change the example: the rescuer is inside a workshop and hears a crash but cannot identify the falling person’s location. The character may shout a warning, move to see, or act on a known place with an appropriate method. They cannot simply claim the same precise rescue as before unless an applicable sense or actual working establishes it. Compare another change: the rope was already secured around a support. That preparation may protect the falling person without requiring the same new reaction. The actual scene determines which opportunity exists.
An exercise in immediate scope

Which proposal is clearest: stop the fall, erase every injury the companion has, or toss the available line? The last already names an ordinary method. The first can become clear by naming a suitable acquired working and its exact recipient. The second combines a rescue with a broader unrelated promise unless the character genuinely has the relevant scope. The answer is not that reactions must be mundane or small. A remarkable response can be valid; it needs a perceived trigger, legitimate access, an intelligible immediate purpose, and an actual remaining opportunity to matter.
Check immediate scope before the roll

The normal reactive scope is an immediate Complexity 0–1 response affecting self/touch or one target. Read it alongside any actual granted exception. An elaborate sequence that first locates a hidden person, constructs a route, moves the whole party, and heals several recipients should not be compressed into an ordinary reaction because the moment is urgent. Separate what is immediately possible from what requires a new intent or further work. The rescue can still be remarkable; its immediate purpose, available slot, trigger, access, and eligible scope must be intelligible before the resolution is chosen.
A failed plan can leave a better question
**Original worked example.** CHANGED SITUATIONS
Apply the agreed result

In this worked example, the party tries to reach a stranded worker across a damaged stair. The table has agreed that a failed crossing could break a loose section while a secured line protects the rescuer from an immediate uncontrolled fall. After resolution, the stair gives way and the line catches. The worker remains stranded. These facts are the new scene. Do not compress them into “nothing happens” or quietly convert them into a different penalty after the roll. The consequence should make sense in relation to the described method and the earlier agreement.
Keep the useful work

The line was secured before the crossing and remains attached under this example’s circumstances. A companion has already identified a sound post, and the warning has brought help to the bank. Those contributions do not vanish merely because the final objective was not yet achieved. Equally, preparation does not guarantee every later task. The rope can be damaged, a post can fail, or someone can remain beyond reach if the actual result establishes that. Record what is true now. Specific aftermath gives players more to work with than a single success-or-failure label.
A conversation from the line

Player: “I am hanging below the landing. Can I see the window on its underside?” DM: “Yes. The broken stair has exposed it.” Companion: “I can hold the line while you ask the worker to open it.” Player: “Then I try to reach that opening.” This exchange does not refund resources or guarantee the new attempt. It follows a changed route that the first plan revealed. The party can appraise reach, support, uncertainty, and consequences again. Their next decision is different because the earlier result changed the place, not because they asked to roll the same sentence until it worked.
When repetition really is a choice

Some tasks allow another attempt: time passes, the method is adjusted, the obstacle remains, and the consequences of trying again are understood. Other results remove the opportunity, reveal that the method cannot work, or demand a different approach. Ask which situation applies. A failed effort to persuade someone may leave new information or damaged trust rather than an unlimited invitation to repeat the same demand. A failed search can narrow the places checked. A broken stair cannot be treated as intact on the next roll just because the character has a favorable total.
Use ambition without hiding a new power

The player now proposes shaping water to lift the rescuer toward the exposed window. Check the actual subject and behavior rather than declaring that failure permits anything cinematic. The Rule of Cool supports discussing an engaging response. If the existing permission fits, appraise this expression and its consequences. If it does not, say what is missing and consider an ordinary route or an explicit contextual agreement. A new consequence may support greater eligible effort; it does not silently buy unrelated access. The scene stays imaginative when those boundaries are understandable.
The exercise: write an aftermath

Choose a task from your own character: negotiating safe passage, repairing a gate, climbing a wall, or locating a missing object. Write a plausible result in which the goal is not achieved but something changes usefully. Then write the next question that result invites. An explanation such as “the gate stays closed, but we discover the hinge was replaced yesterday; who supplied it?” is stronger than “try again.” The answer need not always be favorable. It should be specific enough to carry consequences and decisions forward, with the player still able to understand the shared situation.
A partial result is a specific result

A table may agree that an attempt can produce an intermediate outcome, but the phrase “partial success” is not enough by itself. Say what changed: the worker reaches the landing but the supplies remain above, the stair is braced only while someone holds it, or the route is revealed without being secured. Record the actual consequence and any continuing requirement. The new scene should give the players a meaningful next choice. Do not use an appealing label to conceal an invented result that contradicts the method or the stakes everyone accepted.
Cross without winning a fight
**Original worked example.** NONCOMBAT OBJECTIVES
Name the goal in the place

A herd blocks the safest ford. In this example, the party needs to reach a settlement before supplies run short. Their goal is crossing, not necessarily killing the animals. Ask about the banks, currents, herd movement, young animals, and other possible routes. The DM can describe evident behavior. Players can watch, wait, communicate, distract, guide, or alter their own route according to the actual circumstances and permissions. A creature’s BU and combat record help when those mechanics matter; they do not turn every encounter into a challenge that must end with its defeat.
Look for what the other side protects

The grazers keep returning toward their young and leave a narrow retreat route behind them. That observation suggests a useful approach: give them space rather than crowd the vulnerable part of the herd. It does not grant automatic animal obedience or a universal bonus. The group still needs a method that works in this place. A player with applicable knowledge may interpret behavior; another can inspect the water; another can ensure nobody approaches from behind. Meaningful uncertainty can be resolved with the appropriate practice or other agreed method after the intended contribution is clear.
A conversation on the bank

Player: “We want to cross without separating the young. Can we wait until the adults move?” DM: “They are unsettled because your carts block their route back to the meadow.” Companion: “I move our lead cart away from that path.” Player: “Then I watch for the gap they leave.” These ordinary decisions alter the situation without inventing a new power. The herd may settle or the passage may remain risky under the actual result. The conversation works because the party respects an observable purpose and describes practical changes, rather than demanding an undefined roll to make the animals friendly.
Exceptional solutions have actual subjects

A character might offer a suitable working to redirect water, produce a harmless distraction, or communicate in a granted way. Read exactly what it permits. Owning a broad-sounding nature theme does not automatically command every living creature or rewrite its motives. A distraction can attract attention without controlling what the animal does next. A route shaped through the water still needs to accommodate the people and supplies using it. If the effect involves recipients or a continuing result, establish those terms before companions depend on it. Useful extraordinary access often supports an ordinary plan.
Compare the night crossing

Now change the situation: darkness obscures the far bank and the current has risen. Waiting for the same opening may no longer be enough. The group needs legitimate perception of the route, a sound means of crossing, and a plan for the supplies. A clever daytime solution should not erase new uncertainty. Nor does the changed scene require a fight. The party might shelter, investigate another route, seek local guidance, or negotiate consequences for a demanding attempt. Compare those options against the objective and what the characters actually know, not a compulsory difficulty label.
What counts as progress

The party crosses only the essential medicine and sends someone to find help for the remaining carts. They have not completed the entire journey, but the most urgent need is served. Record who crossed, what remains, and which obligations follow. Other groups might safely wait and lose time, or find a longer route. These can all be meaningful outcomes. For a practice exercise, state the ford scene without mentioning attacks. List three outcomes the party would welcome and one consequence it would accept. That list gives the table more useful directions than a single instruction to clear the encounter.
Take the creatures out of the exercise

Imagine the same ford obstructed by fallen timber instead of a herd. Observation, route selection, cargo handling, time, and the party’s actual access still matter. Now restore the animals and name what changes: motives, movement, young to protect, and possible responses to the party. This comparison helps distinguish a living encounter from a static barrier. The answer should not reduce animals to obedient obstacles or compulsory opponents. A useful encounter gives the party a purpose in a place and lets the creatures’ actual behavior affect how that purpose can be pursued.
Follow evidence through a place
**Original worked example.** INVESTIGATION IN PLAY
A question the site can answer

Someone has altered a warning on a ruined crossing. In this example, a monument attendant remembers repairs and visitors within its actual capabilities. The party wants to know which warning travelers would have seen. Start with that question. The stone, its position, damaged lettering, and nearby tracks may all contain evidence. A mystery becomes easier to investigate when players can name what they are looking for and what a discovery would change. They need not guess the title of a hidden clue or make a generic investigation roll before the place becomes available.
Observation before interpretation

A character notices fresh cuts beneath old weathering. That observation differs from concluding who made them or why. Another recognizes a mason’s mark; another compares the warning to a traveler’s account. Keep those contributions distinct. The DM can establish evident details directly and resolve meaningful uncertainty where it remains. A known clue should not disappear because another character fails a different check. Write it in plain language with its source: “Fresh marks under the replaced warning, observed at the crossing.” This small habit keeps the group’s later reasoning anchored in information it actually has.
The attendant knows something particular

Ask the attendant what it can genuinely recall or perceive. Its age and carved appearance are evocative, but neither grants complete access to every historical event. If the party uses an extraordinary working to read a trace, inspect the actual subject, behavior, scope, and available information. A record of a repair might identify a visitor without revealing their motive. Treat that boundary as an invitation to another lead. Narrow information is valuable when it answers a clear question; it does not need to solve the whole story to justify the method.
A conversation over the lettering

Player: “Can the attendant tell whether the warning changed before the last caravan passed?” DM: “It remembers the repair, but not every departure. What can you compare?” Companion: “The caravan gave us a copied inscription. I put it beside the stone.” Player: “Then we can establish whether they saw the old wording.” This exchange combines a witness and an ordinary object. The comparison can be secure or uncertain according to the actual records. The players are not promised that a successful check makes their favorite suspect guilty. They are making the next decision better informed.
Two routes from the same discovery

The copied warning differs from the stone. One group follows the mason’s mark toward a workshop. Another goes to the caravan to warn it about the route. Both use the discovery, but they serve different priorities. The first seeks responsibility; the second protects travelers. A scene should let those priorities matter. The DM can describe what each route costs in time, exposure, or obligation without inventing a fixed penalty. A player should know the likely tradeoff before choosing. Information opens decisions; it should not always funnel every party into the same next roll.
When the record is incomplete

Change the example: the copied inscription is torn, and the attendant’s account stops before the repair finished. The group can still establish some facts while leaving others unknown. Ask which conclusion is supported and which needs more evidence. A character may choose precautions without certainty. Protecting the caravan does not require first proving a suspect’s motive. Avoid filling a gap with an unlisted supernatural ability or declaring that nothing can be done until the entire mystery is solved. Partial knowledge can be enough to justify a useful and consequential next step.
The exercise: three lines of evidence

Choose a familiar place from your campaign and write an observation, an interpretation, and a next question. For the crossing: “new cuts below old weathering”; “the warning may have been altered after installation”; “who worked here since the caravan left?” The explanation matters: the interpretation follows from a clue but is not identical to it. A different cause might fit. Your next question tests that uncertainty instead of merely restating suspicion. Keep the three lines with the party notes. They make discussion accessible to someone who missed the original scene and help prevent a remembered theory becoming a false established fact.
A bargain is not control
**Original worked example.** NEGOTIATION AND AGENCY
Say what you are offering

A lesser contract spirit disputes a promise that keeps a workshop closed. In this example, the party wants access to a trapped courier without destroying evidence of the agreement. Ask what the spirit claims, what the written terms say, and who is able to change them. A player can offer a new arrangement, uncover a misunderstanding, or challenge an interpretation. This is a negotiation with a purpose. “I roll Influence” does not yet describe what the other side is being asked to accept or why acceptance would make sense to it.
Give the other side a reason

A credible offer connects to something the other party values. The courier can preserve the damaged document, the workshop owner can complete an unfinished delivery, or the group can investigate who replaced a seal. These are example offers, not universal prices. Ask what each side can actually promise. A player cannot guarantee a distant official’s decision without the means to secure it. The spirit need not accept simply because a character has a strong bonus. Applicable resolution addresses meaningful uncertainty in an intelligible attempt, while the actual situation and scope remain relevant.
Words need shared meanings

Before committing to an unusual bargain, clarify the important terms in plain language. Does access mean entering the room, taking the courier away, or removing every protected object? Who must perform the promised task, and when is the obligation fulfilled? This supports a fair dramatic agreement rather than a puzzle built from unstated vocabulary. If a spirit is deliberately literal, make that behavior part of the scene. Players can enjoy careful wording without being expected to foresee a secret definition for every ordinary word. A consequence should be understandable enough to choose.
A conversation about the seal

Player: “We will preserve your record while we take the courier to safety.” DM: “The spirit says removing the courier breaks the named obligation. It will permit a witness to examine the changed seal.” Companion: “Then I ask to inspect it here, with the courier present.” The goal has shifted from immediate extraction toward testing the claim. This is not automatically a failed scene. The offer has revealed a useful boundary. The party can proceed, seek another route, or accept a different obligation after its terms are clear. A character’s personality can shape the offer without replacing its actual content.
Influence does not erase another person

An ordinary social check is not a universal command over someone’s choices, and it should not dictate another player character’s feelings without that player’s participation. Extraordinary compulsion needs its actual acquired rule, recipient, reach, and limits. A title such as commanding presence cannot provide every such outcome. Even a valid supernatural result should be applied according to what it really changes. If it causes one permitted response, do not silently expand that into lifelong loyalty, shared beliefs, or permission to rewrite all later decisions. Keep the character’s actual access visible.
Compare the promise you cannot keep

Now the party proposes retrieving a missing object but knows that it has already been destroyed. That changes the truth and risk of the offer. They may negotiate a substitute, reveal the loss, or make a deceptive attempt with intelligible stakes. The DM should not treat all three methods as identical. A successful lie can change what someone believes without making the promised object exist. The party’s future obligation and the possibility of discovery remain whatever the actual result establishes. Social play becomes useful when its consequences continue into later decisions.
Leave with a playable agreement

Write the final agreement as a short record: the parties, allowed action, obligation, completion condition, and any retained uncertainty. Read it aloud so everyone can correct a misunderstanding. This is especially important when the promise restricts a character’s access or creates a continuing consequence. For an exercise, remove all dramatic titles from the contract scene and explain what each party wants. If the bargain still makes sense, the scene has a strong foundation. If it becomes meaningless, clarify the actual interests before adding more elaborate language or extraordinary effects.
Make travel a shared choice
**Original worked example.** JOURNEYS AND PREPARATION
Why this route matters

A messenger carries a replacement part toward a settlement whose gate is failing. In this example, the party can take a narrow direct route, a safer long road, or a ferry whose operator must be found. Each choice should be described in terms the characters can understand. They may know the road’s condition, have a map, or need more information. There is no need to import a mandatory travel sequence or fixed daily encounter count. Begin with the journey’s purpose and the uncertainty that makes choosing a route interesting.
Divide the questions, not the spotlight

One character asks about terrain, another about supplies, another about people who know the road, and another about the messenger’s deadline. These contributions may use practices, ordinary conversation, or actual extraordinary methods. They need not become separate obligatory rolls every time the party moves. Ask what information is already established and which remaining uncertainty affects the choice. A practical contribution can be as small as noticing that the load will not fit through a passage. Make room for players who prefer a short useful statement instead of a long performance.
A conversation over the map

Player: “The direct route saves time, but can the cart cross its bridge?” DM: “Your map marks a foot crossing. The courier has only used it without a cart.” Companion: “We can carry the essential part and send the cart around with help.” Player: “Then our problem is protecting the smaller load, not widening the bridge.” This example changes the method without inventing an ability. The group should still establish what is carried, who takes which route, and how they will reconnect. Splitting tasks can create new responsibilities rather than automatically solving every logistical concern.
Extraordinary travel is an actual working

If a character proposes flight, rapid movement, a shaped path, or another exceptional method, inspect the real recipients and scope. Carrying the actor does not necessarily carry an entire party, cart, and cargo. A sustained route may need continuing direction or agreed maintenance. An extended range does not automatically locate a distant safe destination. Ask what the character knows about the place and what the method actually requires. A clear ability can make travel wonderfully different without becoming an unlimited answer to every obstacle and every hidden destination.
Keep the cargo in the story

The replacement part is not merely a quest label. Who holds it? Is it fragile, bulky, protected from water, or visible to people seeking it? Record its actual Load and any rule that matters. Item BU is not ordinary purchase price, and a narrative value does not create a mechanical power. The courier can explain how the part fits the gate without granting the party every workshop skill. Treat the object and its delivery as real circumstances. A safe crossing that abandons the cargo may not serve the journey’s purpose.
Compare a changed forecast

Now the party hears that the ferry has stopped because of rising water. The previous route choice can be reconsidered using new information. A character may investigate, negotiate assistance, reduce the load, or accept a delay. The DM can explain the likely consequence of waiting without imposing an unannounced fixed deadline penalty. If urgency is part of the agreement, keep it visible. The players should not be punished for lacking information their characters could reasonably obtain. A journey works well when preparation and new observations both affect the decisions that follow.
What you bring into the next scene

At arrival, note the cargo’s condition, people separated from the party, promises made along the road, and resources genuinely consumed. These facts can make the settlement scene richer. For an exercise, describe the same journey from three priorities: fastest arrival, lowest exposure, and preserving every supply. None is automatically correct. Explain which route serves each priority and what it risks under the known circumstances. This helps players recognize that travel choices belong to their characters’ values as well as their strongest numbers. A successful arrival can still leave an interesting obligation to fulfill.
Carry the things you actually have
**Original worked example.** EQUIPMENT IN USE
A caravan asks a practical question

A damaged axle stops a caravan outside shelter. In this example, a repair automaton can help according to its actual record, but the party still needs to know which parts and tools are available. Start with the object’s condition and the desired result. Is the plan to repair it, support it until help arrives, transfer the cargo, or continue on foot? Each method asks different questions. Owning an impressive item does not prove it contains every tool, while ordinary equipment can solve a problem without extraordinary ingredients.
Carried is not equipped

The equipment record distinguishes what is carried from what is currently in use. Equipped items contribute their actual active rules and slot requirements; carried unequipped objects still contribute Load. A tool can remain available to retrieve without already providing every equipped benefit. The default uses six universal equipped slots, with ordinary items using one and two-handed items two unless an actual rule establishes something else. A particular permitted item can require more, and primitives can extend the available slots. Size alone does not multiply every requirement. Read the final authored record instead of inferring it from the illustration.
Three figures, three questions

Item BU accounts for the mechanics acquired through equipment. Ordinary value concerns trade or the campaign’s economy. Load measures carried burden. These figures can differ greatly: a mundane component may be valuable and awkward without granting an extraordinary rule, while a small device may contain important mechanics. Keep them in separate columns. Moving equipment between characters changes who carries and can use it under its actual terms; it does not erase its existence. A backpack organizes the load but does not automatically increase capacity or make its contents disappear from the record.
A conversation beside the wheel

Player: “I have the brace in my pack. I take it out and support the axle.” Companion: “I can hold the cart while the patchwright works.” DM: “The support gives it a stable place to repair, but the damaged pin must still be replaced.” Player: “Do we have a spare, or can we salvage one from the empty wagon?” The discussion stays concrete. The brace changes the task; it is not a universal repair bonus. The automaton’s actual capacity and the available materials determine which part of the proposed result is possible.
An extraordinary item has actual conditions

If the brace carries a capability, read what activates it, who receives the result, and whether equipping or another condition is required. The item’s subject and behavior do not become the wielder’s owned positive foundation permissions merely because it is in their pack. An item may provide a granted use under its own rule while the character’s acquisition ledger remains distinct. Apply its actual stacking treatment. Two references to the same item benefit in different notes are not two separate equipped objects. A short readable item card should preserve these distinctions rather than only advertise a powerful name.
Compare leaving the cart behind

The party decides to carry the medicine and abandon the broken cart temporarily. Recalculate the actual carried burden and record what remains at the site. The empty cart’s condition can matter when they return. If someone carries another character’s equipment, make that transfer clear instead of granting both characters simultaneous possession. The group can share objects efficiently, but its record should follow the shared fiction. Any encumbrance consequences use the actual capacity and agreed treatment. A logistical choice should be understandable before the party commits, not an unexplained penalty discovered much later.
The exercise: inspect one item

Choose an item your character often uses. Write what it is, who currently holds it, whether it is equipped, its final slot requirement, Load, Item BU, and actual granted rules. Then imagine lending it to a companion. Which entries change, and which remain properties of the object? The holder and equipped state can change; the object’s authored mechanics do not automatically rewrite themselves. This exercise is useful even for a mundane rope. A reliable small inventory lets tools enter play naturally, without turning every practical task into a search through decorative descriptions.
Rest is recovery you agree
**Original worked example.** REST AND RECOVERY
A pause in a real place

The party reaches a sheltered ledge after the crossing. In this example, someone needs recovery, someone watches the route, and the group still has a delivery to finish. Ask what kind of rest the circumstances support. A short rest is a meaningful pause; a long rest is overnight sleep or equivalent recovery, not a compulsory eight-hour timer. DM and players agree whether the effects apply. Simply announcing a duration does not make danger, discomfort, or continuing obligations irrelevant. The useful question is what recovery this actual pause earns.
Only the points restored are spent

Short rests share a finite recovery allowance between completed long rests. Its normal amount is half maximum Vitality, rounded upward. Only actual Vitality restored consumes that allowance. In the worked example, maximum Vitality is 13, so the allowance is 7. The character begins the pause at 10/13. Restoring 3 reaches the maximum and leaves 4 for later agreed short rests. The unused points are not discarded because the character became full. Nor are they extra Vitality stored above the maximum. They remain available recovery, recorded separately from current Vitality.
A conversation at the shelter

Player: “I need only three points to reach my maximum. I record four short-rest recovery left.” DM: “The ledge is sheltered enough for the agreed pause, while your companion watches.” Companion: “I will keep an eye on the stair, then we can switch.” The example establishes a particular recovery agreement; it does not say every lookout arrangement guarantees rest. If continuing a working prevents the actor from resting under its actual requirements, discuss that openly. Another person can help with ordinary shelter or watch without automatically inheriting the actor’s extraordinary maintenance.
The second pause uses the same allowance

After later damage, the character is at 9/13. A second agreed short rest can restore the remaining 4 and reach 13/13, leaving no short-rest recovery in the pool. A third short rest does not automatically create a new allowance. It can still be a useful pause for conversation, preparation, or other agreed purposes. A table adjustment remains available, but should be explicit. The normal rule tracks actual recovery across the interval, rather than granting a fresh half-maximum heal whenever someone says they rest again.
Long rest has its own recovery

A completed long rest normally restores Vitality to the maximum and refreshes the short-rest allowance. Its healing is not charged against the old short-rest pool. Poor sleep or difficult conditions can support a table-agreed partial result. Establish the amount and meaning clearly, applying ordinary upward rounding when a chosen calculation needs it. Do not surprise a player with a secret adjustment after the fact. The completed long rest and its recovery terms are the relevant event; elapsed hours alone do not settle the agreement. Record the resulting current Vitality and refreshed allowance separately.
What rest does not silently erase

A ruined map remains ruined. A lost-access consequence may require a task. An injury may have its own recovery condition. Healing Vitality does not automatically satisfy any of those rules. Read what remains and ask which practical help is available. The party might seek a workshop, make an apology, or arrange assisted recovery. If someone is actively dying, rescue comes before treating a pause as ordinary rest. A stabilized person can recover through assisted rest under the appropriate circumstances, but stabilization itself supplies neither healing nor consciousness.
The exercise: three honest entries

On paper, keep current/maximum Vitality, short-rest allowance remaining, and lasting consequences on separate lines. For the worked example, begin with 10/13 and allowance 7; after the first pause write 13/13 and allowance 4. After the later injury write 9/13 and allowance 4; after recovery write 13/13 and allowance 0. Explain the entries aloud. The important distinction is between a present resource and permission to recover it later. At the next agreed completed long rest, update recovery according to that agreement and refresh the normal allowance without charging its healing to the exhausted short-rest pool.
Rescue before bookkeeping
**Original worked example.** COLLAPSE AND STABILIZATION
Begin with the danger

A companion collapses on a broken landing. In this worked example, the party must reach them while keeping the landing from failing further. At zero Vitality, collapse leaves the character unconscious and incapacitated under the normal rule. The DM establishes contextual rescue stakes. Do not assume a guaranteed sequence of safe rounds while everyone searches a sheet. Ask where the person is, what immediate hazard remains, who can reach them, and what an assisting character can actually do. A short description of those facts makes the next decision clearer than announcing only a resource value.
Divide the urgent work

One companion can protect a route, another can keep an attacker away, another can reach the injured person, and another can attempt stabilization. These are related but different results. Moving someone out of water can remove an immediate hazard without automatically restoring Vitality or halting every dying consequence. Successful stabilization stops the rescue countdown, but it does not heal or wake the character. Actual healing above zero ends the dying state and restores consciousness unless another consequence prevents it. The group should know which result it is attempting before resolving the action.
A conversation on the landing

Player: “I cross the secure section and try to stabilize them.” DM: “The broken rail leaves a clear route if the support holds. What are the others doing?” Companion: “I keep the line taut so they can work safely.” Third player: “I watch the upper doorway.” The table appraises the actual Fieldcraft attempt or a suitable creative use of owned primitives, its timing, uncertainty, and Cost. There is no universal stabilization DC to invent here. The example shows ordinary help making the rescue intelligible, while leaving each attempt’s real resolution to the table.
Healing still needs the actual working

A player who can control water or produce an output die does not automatically gain healing. A rescuer using an extraordinary method must have the subject and behavior that establish that result, as well as legitimate targeting and reach. A restorative name on an item should be read just as carefully. The illustrated guardian’s abilities remain its own actual record. If the character lacks suitable healing access, stabilization and practical protection can still be valuable. Do not dismiss those methods simply because they do not immediately refill the injured person’s Vitality.
Compare an assisted recovery

After stabilization, the party takes the companion to shelter. They can arrange assisted rest under the agreed recovery rules. That differs from attempting to rest while someone remains actively dying. Establish what the stabilized person needs, what consequences persist, and which recovery the circumstances support. Restoring Vitality may wake them while another injury still limits movement. A safe room may remove exposure while leaving an access restriction unchanged. Read those terms separately. This makes recovery a sequence of understandable conditions rather than a single word that silently solves every possible harm.
Do not hide an outright lethal result

The massive-damage rule and explicitly established lethal stakes remain relevant. A sheet that displays zero cannot be used to ignore a lethal overrun in the resolved damage. The contextual opportunity to rescue a collapsed character does not reverse an outright lethal result. Establish such stakes before resolution and apply the actual final damage after relevant defenses. This distinction belongs in preparation for dangerous play, not as a surprise discovered when a player asks for help. The table can discuss desired tone and boundaries while retaining the system’s real consequences.
The exercise: what changed?

Read these four results separately: the injured person is moved away from the edge; stabilization succeeds; healing raises Vitality above zero; an agreed completed rest restores further Vitality. Explain each result without substituting one for another. Moving changes location and immediate exposure. Stabilization halts the rescue countdown. Healing can end the dying state and restore consciousness, subject to other consequences. Rest uses its agreed recovery and allowance rules. The answer preserves the rescue’s actual stages. A party that can state them plainly is better equipped to coordinate help without wasting the scene on confused resource bookkeeping.
Grow from the scene you remember
**Original worked example.** ADVANCEMENT AND REVISION
A reason to learn something

A character returns from the bridge rescue remembering a limit: they could guide the water but could not locate someone beyond the wall. In this example, the player wants that experience to influence future acquisitions. They might pursue an appropriate sense, train a useful practice, improve a known working, or learn to prepare better ordinary tools. Advancement does not require abandoning the character’s identity for a prescribed career. Ask which recurring problem the character now cares about and what actual rule or practical habit would make their next contribution more understandable.
Budget and purchases are different records

The progression reference gives a cumulative acquisition allowance. The purchase ledger records what the character has actually acquired. Do not add a cumulative table value to the previous allowance as if it were an increment, and do not count spent BU as a new second progression total. Ordinary unspent BU, valid mirror credit, and actual debt used remain distinct. Item BU stays separate. The DM and players agree rewards and pacing; there is no compulsory per-session schedule that must be invented to make a campaign function. State which progression reference and agreement the table uses.
A conversation after the rescue

Player: “I want to learn a sense that could locate someone behind a partition.” DM: “Describe the information and medium you want. What blocks it?” Player: “I imagine contact through a continuous surface, not reading thoughts or seeing all equipment.” Companion: “Then we can compare it with the existing contact-sense examples.” The proposed acquisition is still reviewed for its actual scope and price. The scene supplies a reason to learn, not automatic permission. A narrow intelligible grant can serve the concept more reliably than a powerful title whose limits nobody can explain.
Reorganizing is not repurchasing

The player gives an existing working a clearer capability name and moves its references into a heritage reflecting new responsibilities. If no actual acquisition changed, the underlying purchase count does not multiply. If the new record adds a sense, numerical bonus, or other genuine rule, record that addition and its agreed accounting. Keep a note of the adopted version where it matters. Rewriting a biography can alter what the character values without granting extra mechanics; replacing an ingredient can alter mechanics without requiring the entire biography to disappear. Review the two kinds of change separately.
A drawback must remain a real choice

A player may propose an eligible personal drawback with mirror credit. Read its actual consequence, recipient, condition, and ending terms. A descriptive dislike does not automatically produce budget. A debt ceiling limits what may be used; it is not free credit. Reusing the drawback inside several compositions does not erase it or create unlimited new credit. An ally’s benefit does not remove a restriction on the character who accepted it. These distinctions help the group assess whether the drawback will genuinely appear in play. If it will not, revise the proposal instead of treating accounting as a substitute for agreement.
The sheet grows, but does not heal itself

When advancement changes derived values, review the actual current attributes, applicable training, defenses, and maximum Vitality. Raising maximum Vitality does not automatically restore current Vitality. An explicit bonus has its own conditions; a proficiency grant does not become another copy of PB merely because the character already has training. If a new acquisition introduces advantage, use the net-stack rule rather than folding it into an unexplained numerical modifier.
