A short before-and-after review catches practical misunderstandings while preserving the useful history of how the character learned.
The exercise: choose one next lesson

Name a scene your character recently struggled with. Write the desired improvement, an existing or proposed ingredient that genuinely supports it, and one limit that remains afterward. For the bridge rescuer, a contact sense may improve location through its stated medium while leaving reach, delivery, and healing unchanged. Explain a future use and a use outside its scope. Then check the purchase ledger and table agreement. The answer should connect story, actual permission, and accounting. You do not need to solve every future problem at once; one well-understood acquisition can make the next adventure feel different.
Play with paper, not a second app
**Original worked example.** ACCESSIBLE TABLE RECORDS
Keep the information a human needs

You can play without the platform open. In this example, the party takes paper records to a table with limited space. The useful character page holds current values, applicable check totals, owned permissions, important equipment, and active consequences. Supporting pages preserve actual ingredient definitions and version notes where needed. A list of impressive names alone is not enough to explain a working. Conversely, printing every public catalogue entry is unnecessary. Choose the content the character actually uses and make it available in a form its player can comfortably read.
Three records prevent confusion

Separate the enduring character record, the purchase ledger, and the scene state. The character record explains actual rules and current derived values. The ledger identifies acquisitions and separate Item BU accounting. Scene state tracks current Vitality, movement used, Reaction Slot availability, active workings, and consequences. These can fit on one sheet or several, depending on the reader. Their separation is conceptual, not a compulsory page count. Erasing a spent reaction should not accidentally delete an acquired rule; renaming a capability should not erase a consequence still affecting the character.
A conversation before play

Player: “My working card has the ingredient definitions on the back. Here is the normal use, and here is the targeting limit.” Companion: “Can I read that limit aloud when we plan?” Player: “Yes. My scene note tracks whether it is currently maintained.” The table has enough information to discuss a future use. This example does not require every player to perform a speech or expose private character notes. It shows how a short readable record can support cooperation. A player may prefer a quiet written description, a spoken summary, or another comfortable way of sharing the necessary facts.
Show position without a compulsory map

For a complicated crossing, sketch the bank, landing, line, and known recipients. Label what blocks sight or delivery and which support is secure. For a conversation, a short list of people and promises may be more useful than a battle map. Use the representation that explains the actual uncertainty. A rough drawing need not introduce precise grid mechanics the table has not adopted. If someone cannot see the diagram, describe the relevant relationships aloud. The shared scene is the important result; the drawing is a tool to help everyone understand it.
Make changing state easy to change

Use a pencil, tokens, separate cards, or another familiar method for temporary state. A token can show a spent Reaction Slot; a short note can show the next upkeep point and ending condition. Spell out the token’s meaning rather than expecting everyone to recognize a color. Keep current and maximum Vitality distinct, alongside the short-rest recovery still available. Write actual ending conditions for lasting consequences. A new Council clears the appropriate round markers, not every persistent restriction. This prevents a tidy table from becoming a mechanically misleading table.
Adjust the presentation to the player

Someone may need larger text, stronger contrast, more room between lines, or a spoken explanation. Someone else may prefer a compact card with details on a second sheet. These changes need not remove rules or change the character. Avoid using decorative script for long instructions or relying on an illustration to convey a necessary limit. Read an important agreement aloud if that helps, and let the player verify the record. Accessible play comes from making the actual information available without demanding the same reading speed, memory, or style of performance from every person.
The exercise: hand over one working

Give a companion the record of one frequently used capability without explaining it first. Ask them to identify the subject, behavior, targeting method, reach, continuing terms, and actual consequence. If they cannot find an answer, improve the record or include the missing ingredient definition. Do not ask them to guess from the artwork or title. Next, show the separate purchase entry and explain which references point to that same acquisition. The exercise succeeds when another human can apply the real working in a changed scene. A beautiful record is most useful when its beauty makes those answers easier to find.
Topic index
Use this alphabetical index for a rule, construction procedure or worked example. PDF page numbers and links refer to this edition; web links go directly to the section.

title: Game Master's Guide
subtitle: Prepare situations. Make clear rulings. Let choices matter.
description: Run your first session, review creations, author creatures and prepare encounters with practical worksheets.

blocks.text: Rules edition: **v0.1 alpha** · 12 October 2026 · Free digital edition.
Begin with a playable situation

You do not need a map of a continent to run your first SwordWeave session. You need people who want something, a situation that will change if nobody intervenes, and enough facts to respond to the players' ideas. Prepare the pressure, then let their choices determine the story.

The Player's Handbook teaches the shared procedures; the SRD states them precisely. This guide helps you apply them: agree a ruling, review a creation, give a creature a purpose, prepare an encounter and keep a campaign moving. “Dungeon Master” and “Game Master” mean the same role here. You are also a player, with the world and its other inhabitants as your responsibilities.
What to bring to the first session

Bring the shared rules, a way to record changes, the dice your table uses, and character records. Digital sheets are convenient; paper records work. Establish who can edit shared digital sheets rather than assuming that viewing permission grants editing permission.

Agree the starting budget and equipment, the tone, the expected length of play, and boundaries for content and interpersonal behavior. Discuss character concepts together. A group with a reason to cooperate gives the first scene somewhere to go. A 25-BU starting character is a default, not a promise that every newly invented power is accepted without review.

**Optional guidance.** Ask each player for a reason to help the others and a question they want the campaign to answer. Agree an easy way to pause or remove uncomfortable material without requiring personal explanations. Revisit that agreement as the game changes. This is table care, not a mechanical character cost.

Before play, check that everyone knows their current Vitality, applicable check bonuses, movement, reaction slot, relevant permissions and how their capabilities end. Do not require memorizing the entire Market. Ask a new player to explain one working in their own words; resolve ambiguity together.
A first session: the gate that will not open

**Original example adventure.** The party reaches a canal settlement as water rises against a jammed sluice. Workers need the pressure released. Two Canal Watchers guard a spawning bed downstream and believe opening the gate will destroy it. A maintenance passage can bypass the stuck mechanism, but nobody has checked it since the last flood.

Tell the players what their characters can immediately perceive: brown water climbs the marked gauge; a rope trembles across the channel; workers argue on the bank; one Watcher gestures urgently toward the spawning beds. Begin with “What do you do?” rather than demanding a roll to notice the entire scene.
Prepare these facts, not a mandatory order of events:

rows: What you can reveal and use
Wants colleagues safe; knows the maintenance passage; will explain it to someone who asks
Want safe flow over the beds; can accept a credible diversion; use the complete record in Worked records
Jammed by a snapped timber, not magically sealed; accessible from the bank with suitable tools or a supported working
Narrow, wet and partly obstructed; offers another approach if inspected
Visibly worsens as time and actions pass; give warning before a route becomes unusable
Repair, diversion, evacuation, negotiation or force can change the situation

blocks.text: There is no compulsory sequence of persuasion, fight and repair. If the players recruit the workers, negotiate with the Watchers and divert a narrow channel, let those preparations matter. If they leave, decide where the water goes and which people need help next. The situation continues without requiring them to follow your intended solution.
Teach the first resolution in full

Suppose a character wants to identify the jam. First establish their approach and opportunity. From the safe bank, close inspection might make the broken timber obvious. If they must diagnose it while water shakes the mechanism, uncertainty and risk are meaningful.

**Example ruling.** You agree a Reason check, DC 12, to identify the jam before a support shifts. A player with Mental 3 and applicable PB 2 rolls 8: 8 + 3 + 2 = 13. They identify the timber. They have not automatically removed it. Describe the useful fact and invite the next decision.

DC 12 is this example's agreed target, not a universal repair difficulty. If their displayed combined bonus is +5, use 8 + 5 rather than adding the attribute and training again. If failure would not change anything and there is time to inspect safely, you may simply give the information. A die roll should answer a question the scene actually asks.
End with changed circumstances

After the immediate crisis, ask what the characters did about the beds, the workers and the broken mechanism. Those answers provide the next session's material. Ressa can become an ally; a damaged storehouse can become an obligation; an exposed old channel can reveal a mystery. A fight need not be the event that earns attention or progress.

**Optional guidance.** End the first session with a short review: what was easy to understand, what slowed play, which rule needs clarification, and what each character wants next. Agree rewards and new acquisitions with the table. There is no mandatory XP-per-fight or BU-per-session schedule.
Make rulings people can understand

SwordWeave's DIY nature makes clear conversation more useful than a secret exhaustive list of legal actions. A player describes an outcome; you help establish what makes it possible and what matters if they attempt it. Keep the ordinary world available: a character can climb, negotiate, investigate or improvise without buying a primitive for every everyday act.
Choose the resolution question

rows: Is the result ordinary and secure under these circumstances?
Describe it; no roll is needed merely because an action occurred
Can one actor succeed against an uncertain challenge?
An agreed attribute/practice check against a DC
A clash, using actual timing and context
Does an attack connect or does a recipient resist a working?
The chosen attack or saving-throw procedure; not both automatically
Does a creation permit the proposed behavior?
Read its access and limits before appraising execution

blocks.text: Use the relevant current attribute directly. Training adds applicable PB; expertise uses twice PB where granted. Opposing bias cancels one-for-one; remaining stacks add resolution dice. There is no imported automatic natural-20 success, natural-1 failure or critical multiplier. State any table variation before relying on it.
Present the stakes before commitment

Say what success accomplishes, what the agreed uncertainty concerns, and what failure or Cost would change. A player can narrow or revise an attempt. “You can cross now, but the route is exposed; if the guard wins the timing clash, they can close it first” is clearer than revealing that restriction after the roll.

Separate access from effort. A water-shaping character may attempt a demanding diversion within their permissions. Paying a large Cost does not silently grant resurrection, mind reading or a new domain. If their idea needs a missing ingredient, discuss acquiring it, borrowing an actual source, choosing another approach or agreeing a clearly bounded Rule of Cool exception.

**Optional guidance.** If a failed check would only prompt the same unchanged roll again, advance time, reveal a different obstacle, offer another approach or simply resolve the safe repetition. Do not secretly convert every failure into a new penalty. Choose the stakes together when the scene can support them.
Ordinary obstacles and unusual powers

A lock's material, mechanism, condition and accessibility matter. Ordinary tools may be enough. A metal permission may support reshaping a metal part; a precise internal modification may need a different verb scope from striking the lock. Creating a key, persuading the keeper and breaking the door remain separate approaches.

Targeting requires locating the target through an applicable sense. A player who cannot locate a hidden creature may propose affecting a known spot or area. They must accept the uncertainty that it is empty. Authored scrying, broad weather control or “any qualifying target within range” can define an exception; read its actual limits. Range alone supplies neither vision nor a targeting lock.

Projected workings travel through an actual path. Minor obstruction gives -2 accuracy; standard half cover -4; total cover blocks the trajectory. Direct manifestation does not use those intervening projected-cover penalties, but still requires valid targeting and access. Neither mode guarantees hitting someone whose location is unknown.
Social scenes are encounters too

Know what each participant wants, fears and can reasonably offer. A persuasive argument can change their decision without supernatural control. A check can resolve uncertainty about an approach; it does not automatically rewrite every belief or remove another person's agency. If a capability truly overrides agency or information, its specific permission, recipients, resolution and ending terms need review.

**Example.** A Watcher wants the beds protected. Showing a viable diversion addresses that concern. Threatening it answers a different question and may create hostility. The same Influence bonus does not make those outcomes identical. A good proposal can remove the need for a roll if the response is already clear.
Exploration needs observable choices

Describe signs of danger and resources that can support a plan: cracking supports, wind direction, an unstable floor, a route that is closing, a witness with partial information. Do not hide all useful information behind checks. A failed search should not erase something a character can plainly see.

Distance, time, terrain and supplies can matter without becoming a mandatory new subsystem. If the table wants a travel procedure, define what a decision covers, what is consumed and what constitutes progress. Mark that procedure as a campaign choice; do not present an invented ration tariff or weather table as universal SwordWeave law.
Record exceptions without building a trap

When Rule of Cool supports something unusual, record what made it possible. A Small character might wield an oversized sword with a three-slot requirement or an agreed restriction. That does not grant every Small character unlimited gear or imply a size multiplier for ordinary equipment slots. The fiction and explicit agreement explain the case.

If a ruling proves awkward, discuss a revision between scenes. Keep ownership, purchases and ongoing consequences understandable. Avoid changing a power's meaning silently while a player commits to using it. Campaign consistency supports creativity; it need not freeze an unclear first draft forever.
Direct a shared round

Council → Fast → Measured → Heavy is a shared rhythm, not a row of personal turns. The useful question is how the participants' intentions interact. Make the opposition legible, let the party coordinate, then resolve the dependencies that actually arise.
Council: establish the moving parts

Describe visible positions, immediate pressures and the opposition's apparent intent. Confirm ongoing requirements at their agreed continuation point, reset ordinary reaction availability for the new round, and gather the party's coherent Main Intents. Ask about dependencies: who needs a path, who supplies it, who might interrupt it?

Place actions by complexity: 0-1 in Fast, 2-3 in Measured, 4+ in Heavy. Complexity concerns dependencies, not simply the amount of damage or the BU price. A high-output direct action can be fast; a modest result with several dependent parts can resolve later.
Resolve intersections, not a checklist of isolated attacks

**Annotated example.** At the sluice, Mira wants to divert a narrow flow; Neri wants to carry the snapped timber clear once the pressure falls; a Watcher wants to drive Neri away. The table places the immediate Watcher attack in Fast and the dependent repair in Measured. Mira's required preparation is made explicit before the repair can use it.

If Neri tries to reach the timber before the Watcher closes the route, resolve a timing clash where their opposing intents meet. Each rolls d20 with the suitable attribute, applicable PB and modifiers. Highest goes first; a tie is simultaneous or resolved from stronger fictional position as agreed. Losing timing does not erase Neri's entire intent. They can pivot to a different reachable approach if the changed scene supports it.

If Mira and the Watcher directly oppose control of the same current, a contest can determine whose effort prevails. The question is now force/control, not merely timing. Choose suitable approaches and apply the actual permissions and stakes. Do not call every opposed roll “initiative.”
Reactions interrupt the moment, not the whole round

A default independent reaction has one available slot per round, a valid perceived trigger, immediate Complexity 0-1 and self/touch or a single target scope. Pause the triggering event, resolve the response and continue from what changed. Spending the slot does not guarantee canceling the event or create unlimited reach.

**Example.** Neri catches a worker slipping beside them. Their proximity and available hands support the action. Catching workers on both distant banks is a different scope. A separate authored grant may change reaction capacity or permitted behavior; it must be in the creature/character record.
Movement and position stay continuous

Use each participant's whole-round movement allowance. A Medium character with 30 ft can move 10 in Fast and 20 in Measured; they do not regain 30 because a reaction occurs. Ordinary swim/climb use half walking speed rounded up. Flight/burrowing need actual permission and speed.

Agree extra movement through an acquired rule or an appropriate Cost. Where the situation permits, movement may accompany an intent or occur independently. Positions should answer practical questions about reach, paths and interference. A grid is optional; consistent distances or zones with agreed translations can also work.
Track what will matter next

rows: Shows what is trying to happen and what depends on it
Determines reach, available routes and remaining movement
Prevents accidentally responding several times without a grant
Distinguishes injury from the build's ceiling
Records actual penalties, restrictions and their ending conditions
Records each capability's requirement and next continuation point
Shows progress, warning signs and changed options
A convenience for the current round; not a permanent condition

blocks.text: Advancing a digital phase does not apply damage, expire effects or edit another player's sheet. Review actual endings before moving on. At the next Council, clear previous-round intent/resolved markers and establish the new situation. Keep consequences that have not ended.

**Optional surprise treatment.** Prepared enemies may complete a round before surprised participants respond, depending on the situation or an agreed roll. This is a suggestion, not a compulsory surprise mechanic or an automatic reward for every ambush.
Rescue is part of the scene

At zero Vitality a character collapses. A contextual rescue countdown-roughly a minute as guidance-creates urgency; it is not ten guaranteed safe rounds. Make the danger clear. Stabilization uses an action track, a suitable Fieldcraft approach or actual primitives, agreed resolution and Cost. No universal stabilization DC is prescribed.

Successful stabilization stops dying without granting healing or consciousness. Healing above zero normally ends dying and wakes the character unless another consequence prevents it. Active dying requires rescue before assisted rest. Massive damage can be outright lethal: establish those stakes in advance and use final post-defense damage and the current value before any zero clamp.
Review creations and choose consequences

SwordWeave gives players a construction language. Your job is to help the table understand what a creation does, how it fits the world and what a particular attempt puts at risk. An unusual idea is an invitation to examine the situation. Begin with the result the player wants.

**Core rule.** Establish access, actual scope, stakes, resolution and consequences before commitment. Let the player clarify or revise their intent. Apply the agreed outcome, then continue from the changed situation. The Rule of Cool supports coherent and exciting exceptions; state their scope so an exceptional moment does not accidentally become an unrelated permanent ability.
A review you can use at the table
Read a proposed component with its author. Ask these questions of the definition; do not make a player fill out a form to perform every ordinary action.

rows: What changes, who benefits and who or what can be affected?
Which owned ingredients support the change? Is any proposed behavior absent from them?
When does it apply? What prevents it? What does a broad phrase such as “protected” mean here?
Which ingredients are actual acquisitions and which are references to purchases already counted?
Do additional occurrences apply? Do sources share a uniqueness restriction? Is a grant being confused with another numerical bonus?
How does the actor perform it, and what uncertainty requires resolution?
Does it end immediately, last for a stated duration, or require maintenance? What can interfere?
What suggested BU acquisition price fits this table's scope and restrictions? Keep Item BU separate.

blocks.text: An author's price is a proposal. Library and builder suggestions are useful comparisons. You may accept the proposal or ask for an adjustment, including a cheaper version if its limits make the original price excessive. Explain which part creates the concern. “It affects every target without discrimination or effort” is actionable feedback; “that sounds overpowered” leaves the author guessing.

Keep acquisition and execution separate. A purchased ingredient can support many uses without being bought again. A broad or hurried use can still incur Strain and agreed Cost. Buying another ingredient is one way to establish missing access; increasing effort alone does not silently grant a new behavior.
Review a water-working

**Example.** Mira owns Verb II, a Water domain permission, Near Range and d8 output. She proposes redirecting ordinary water away from a broken canal gate. Read the actual permissions. Check the water's quantity, distance, resistance and where it will go. Moving water is one question; creating a new permanent gate, locating an unseen saboteur or healing a wounded worker are different results.

For a small flow with time to work, you might agree negligible Cost and no roll. In a collapsing sluice, redirecting the whole surge before it reaches the workers is a demanding attempt. Make its reach, recipients, timing and stakes explicit. Mira can narrow the channel she controls, enlist another character or accept a continuing restriction instead of forcing the whole result at once.

Do not charge her again for the Water permission because it appears in both an effect and its parent capability. Do not assume the d8 ingredient makes every manipulation deal damage. Output applies when an appropriate authored construction and the proposed use establish damage or healing.
Write a consequence people can use

A consequence should change decisions at the table. It can be damage, a mechanical penalty, a restriction, lost access, an obligation, exposure, an environmental change or another narrative result. A number is useful where the result is numerical. An understandable restriction is useful where a number would hide what happened.
**Core rule.** Record the actual consequence, its cause, applicable timing or trigger and how it ends. A familiar name does not import another game's condition package.

rows: Mira keeps the surge diverted while the workers repair the gate.
She must keep directing that channel and cannot use this working for a separate water manipulation at the same time.
While she continues the channel; the table agrees its place in the shared round.
Losing the necessary access or being unable to continue the directing task threatens it. A wound alone is not a universal cancellation rule.
The restriction ends when she releases the channel or the repair removes the need for it.

blocks.text: This is a possible ruling for this scene. It does not establish a universal one-capability limit. Several maintained capabilities can coexist; their agreed requirements and costs accumulate. Multiple effects inside one maintained capability share its one upkeep track and one Strain appraisal.
Contrast three possible costs before choosing one:

items: **Mechanical:** an agreed amount of Vitality or a stated numerical penalty.
**Restrictive:** hands, voice, attention or access must remain committed to the task.
**Narrative:** the diversion floods a storehouse, draws attention or leaves a debt to the workers whose route is blocked.

blocks.text: These may combine, but piling on every category is not an automatic measure of fairness. Match the actual effort and scene. Offer a smaller scope or a different approach when a player dislikes the proposed trade-off. Maintaining a working can spread pressure across time and generally be cheaper upfront than forcing a larger result in one execution; there is no compulsory discount formula.

**Alpha rule pending - damage-triggered Vitality upkeep.** Additional repayment triggered by incoming damage, including threshold and counter/reset/excess handling, is undecided. This edition does not impose that numerical scheme. Agree any temporary table treatment explicitly. Ordinary continuation requirements remain usable; this does not change non-Vitality upkeep.
Build creatures that change the scene

A creature is useful when its behavior gives the party something to understand and respond to. Write what it wants, how it acts, what reveals its methods and when it stops fighting. A numerical baseline helps construct it; a purpose makes it playable.
Choose a foundation and check the arithmetic

For positive creature budget B, use rank r = sqrt(B/25), base attribute points ceil(3r), PB 1 + ceil(r), and baseline Vitality max(1, ceil(B/2)). Allocate the available nonnegative points among Physical, Mental and Magical. Resolve explicit authored modifications after the foundation. Do not use the player's 10-point starting allocation or level Vitality formula for this creature baseline.

Choose the proficient attribute and relevant acquired training. Check current values, practices, saves, DC, movement and senses. A high title or budget grants neither immunity nor extra actions. Give every ability its actual ingredients and readable behavior. The Canal Watcher record later in this book is complete, with definitions, totals, check bonuses and two useful workings.
Give the creature a small readable repertoire

**Optional design guidance.** Start with one recognizable signature behavior, one practical alternate approach and a reason to change tactics. A creature that controls a passage and retreats when its nest is safe can create more play than a long list of nearly identical damage powers.

For each ability, record what it does, the eligible targets, access, range, delivery, typical expression, chosen resolution and ending/continuation terms. Its normal expression is a starting use, not an unconditional entitlement to any amount of scaling. If it has an additional action, reaction or special rhythm, write the grant explicitly.
Roles suggest behavior, not hidden bonuses

rows: What route or person does it threaten?
A visible approach, space to retreat or a competing objective
What path and target location does it use?
Cover, interrupted sight, movement or interference
A way around it, a motive to address or a limited defense scope
What does it know and how does it conceal itself?
Detectable signs and a consequence of revealing its position
Clear scope, conditions and an ending or counter-approach
Who benefits and what sustains the help?
A visible dependency the party can disrupt or negotiate
How does it interact with several coordinated intents?
Explicit action economy, readable tells and meaningful objectives

blocks.text: Do not assign a role and silently add a bonus. Actual mechanics belong in actual definitions. If a resistance applies only to Magical Fire, an ordinary Physical attack is not reduced by that label. If a transformation changes appearance, it does not automatically copy a target's abilities.
Test three situations

Before publishing, test the creature's ordinary use, a situation favoring its strengths and a situation exposing its limits. Check whether the proposed actions need missing access. Check quantities, Item BU, actual defenses, upkeep and termination. Ensure privately sourced dependencies are not exposed through a public template.

In the platform, preserve the selected immutable version. A template is reusable; a play copy records one creature's current state. Two copies of the same Watcher should not share damage or consequences. Updating the public template should not secretly rewrite an existing run's pinned content.
Prepare encounters around choices

An encounter is a situation with participants and competing aims. It can be social, exploratory, combative or several of those at once. Prepare what is happening and what will change; give the party more than one possible useful decision.
Write a one-screen preparation

Record a name, a short opening description, the objective/pressure, useful environmental facts and the participants' motivations. Add the chosen templates, pinned versions and quantities. Record Party BU and Party Item BU separately; party size is optional. Linked characters are a convenience, not a requirement.

Manual totals are the primary workflow. If you calculate from linked owned/shared characters, inspect each contribution and explicitly apply the result. Refresh on demand when sheets change; do not silently rewrite a saved preparation. A shared character's visibility does not give permission to change their gameplay state.
Read the budget comparison honestly

Enemy monster BU is the chosen base budget multiplied by quantity. Enemy Item BU is the resolved equipment budget multiplied by quantity. Do not add mirror credit as another creature budget, and do not count equipment in both columns.

**Worked comparison.** Two 25-BU Watchers with no equipment yield 50 creature BU and 0 Item BU. A party with 50 Party BU and 8 Party Item BU totals 58. Enemy combined total is 50: enemy minus party -8; ratio 50/58, about 0.86. With two party members, creature counts match. Each Watcher holds half the enemy creature budget.

These facts are not an “easy” rating. Water control in a narrow sluice, an exposed approach, an evacuation task or a successful negotiation can matter more than that difference. Look for concentrated output, control, area effects, support and burst opportunities. Comparable BU totals do not guarantee comparable difficulty.
Choose a group or shuffle one

Choose creatures for the scene's purpose, or use a suggested group as a starting point. If shuffling, specify whether a BU limit applies per creature or to the whole group. An optional separate boss maximum and Item BU limit answer different questions. Review the resulting group before accepting it; a random roster is not automatically a coherent encounter.

If the budget is missing, you can still save and run the scene. Omit comparisons you cannot calculate. If party size is unknown, do not pretend to know whether the enemies outnumber them. If a ratio has zero or absent party denominator, show the totals rather than a fabricated ratio.
Offer pressure that can be seen

**Optional preparation tool.** Track a visible problem through a few named stages, such as rising, spilling and breaking. Describe what advances it and what can reverse it. This is a scene-specific clock, not an imported universal round timer. Tell the players about warnings before a consequential boundary arrives.

The sluice can rise while participants argue, spill after a support breaks and change routes when the walkway floods. A successful diversion can stop that pressure. Avoid advancing it merely because someone asked a rules question out of character.
Start, resume and conclude

Starting a digital encounter creates one independent private play copy per creature at the pinned preparation version. Repeated creatures get readable names. Resume continues an existing run; starting another run creates fresh copies and preserves the earlier one. Do not confuse opening a template preview with starting a run.

Conclude when the scene's practical question has changed or been answered, not only when all enemies reach zero. End the run while preserving the records. Deleting a preparation does not delete its playable copies. The template remains reusable; a new run need not inherit the previous creatures' damage.
Consequences, recovery and continued play

The review chapter explains writing a consequence. In play, keep its actual effect visible and give the player a way to understand its duration or ending. A dramatic injury, an obligation, lost access or an exposed location can matter without being converted into more damage.
Match the consequence to the attempt

If the character strains to hold a beam, exhaustion or committed hands can fit. If they redirect water, flooding another area can fit. If they openly expose forbidden magic, witnesses or obligations can fit. These are examples; agree the applicable consequence before commitment rather than selecting a surprise punishment afterward.

A 0-6 Strain grade helps discuss the demand; it is not a compulsory Vitality invoice. Scale, impact, complexity, conditions, opposition and urgency matter. A normal use can have negligible Cost. Maintaining a result can distribute pressure instead of demanding the whole expression upfront, but there is no universal discount.
Recovery does not erase every story

DM and players agree whether rest effects apply. A short pause may be 15 or 30 minutes; a long rest is overnight sleep or equivalent recovery, not necessarily eight hours. Time alone does not trigger healing.

The short-rest allowance is half maximum Vitality, rounded up, across short rests until a completed long rest refreshes it. Only actual healing consumes it. At maximum 13, allowance 7: healing from 10 to 13 consumes 3 and leaves 4 for a later rest. Long-rest healing is separate, normally to full; partial recovery may be agreed, and completed long rest still refreshes the short-rest allowance.

An injured hand may need treatment or a specified recovery condition even after Vitality is restored. A promise remains until fulfilled. State those ending terms rather than relying on a vague “rest removes it.” If a consequence is meant to recover quickly, say so.
Keep maintained work understandable

Record each maintained capability, its continuation point, requirement and ending terms. One capability has one upkeep track even with several effects; several capabilities can coexist and their requirements accumulate. Loss of access until a task is completed follows that condition, rather than disappearing at the next Council.

A hit alone does not universally cancel a working. Interference requires actual access, timing and resolution. If the actor cannot perform a required task, they cannot continue it. A completed instant action cannot be interrupted retroactively, although its continuing result may be disrupted by a valid new action.

The numerical question of additional Vitality upkeep repayment triggered by damage is explicitly pending in the review chapter. Keep ordinary agreed continuation usable and do not silently impose an unresolved threshold.
Build adventures from what people do

An adventure can be a short situation, a chain of related encounters or a region of unresolved pressures. Prepare the relationships that let choices matter. You can sell or share adventures while the mechanical framework and official playable options stay openly available.
A compact adventure record

**Optional preparation format.** Write the premise, three people/groups with aims, a few useful locations, an opening pressure, clues to the actual situation and possible changes if nobody acts. List any necessary component definitions or platform collection links. Include the definitions needed offline rather than forcing a reader to purchase another book to use a mechanical option.

For the canal adventure, a merchant wants the route reopened, a river community wants the spawning beds safe and a repair crew wants reliable support. Their aims can align or conflict. The old channel, damaged sluice and settlement storehouse connect those aims. An adventure grows from which relationship the party changes first.
Reveal information through several approaches

If understanding the cause is important, make it discoverable through more than one sensible route: inspection, a witness, physical evidence or an appropriate working. A clue should provide something actionable, not merely announce that another clue exists. A missed check can change the route or stakes without making the entire story unreachable.

Do not promise that every method gives identical detail. Tremorsense, a witness and a document can provide different useful facts. Extraordinary knowledge still needs its actual permission. A high roll does not invent access that the approach never supplied.
Let outcomes leave different worlds

If the party repairs the sluice with the Watchers' help, the settlement gains allies. If they evacuate and abandon it, the route may remain closed. If they destroy the Watchers and release the pressure, the spawning beds may be harmed. These possibilities are not prewritten ending gates; they explain how the world responds to actual choices.

**Optional guidance.** Prepare the next scene from the unresolved consequences, not by restoring the original situation so that your planned fight still occurs. Ask players which thread interests them. A campaign can follow their growing creations and relationships as much as a published plot.
Rewards and long campaigns

Agree advancement pacing and BU awards. No compulsory class table, spell list or encounter XP formula is required. Spending BU buys acquisitions without undoing level progression. Keep equipment BU separate. At higher levels use the literal cumulative thresholds and continuing bracket procedure, not an improvised +10-only replacement.

Invite players to author or refine abilities between sessions. Review the same questions as at creation: scope, recipients, conditions, stacking, actual purchases and Costs in use. Check mirrored drawbacks rather than treating the debt ceiling as automatic free credit. A campaign's changing fiction can support a new heritage, obligation, training or capability without forcing a class label.
Publish reusable material clearly

Distinguish an original definition from a reused ingredient and keep provenance/version references. Public creations need publicly accessible dependencies; a private source should not leak through a published record. Public, followers-only and private visibility describe access to content, not new ownership or gameplay editing rights.

For compatible publications based on SwordWeave's openly licensed text, credit the system, link the license and identify changes. You may sell your own compatible work under the applicable licenses without paying a SwordWeave royalty. Clearly separate your original protected adventure text/art from openly designated mechanical material. Do not imply official endorsement or use another creator's assets without permission.
Prepare a first session people can enter

A first session should let new players make useful decisions before they understand every family of primitive. Prepare a visible problem, a few people with clear motives, and several plausible approaches. Teach the procedure as those approaches arise. You do not need to perform every rule in one evening.
Before anyone makes a character

Tell the group what kind of situation you are offering. “A canal settlement needs help before a storm” gives players more useful direction than a long list of permitted ancestries. Discuss tone, interpersonal expectations, subjects to avoid, and an easy way to pause or revise a scene. Nobody needs to justify a personal boundary in public.

Agree the starting progression budget, equipment allowance, and whether example constructions are accepted. A 25-BU start is useful for learning because the ledger is small. It is not compulsory. Do not promise that every possible capability at an example price will be valid in this campaign.

Ask for a purpose, a connection, and one ordinary competence from each character. A reason to cooperate can be small: shared employment, a borrowed boat, or an interest in the same missing person. They need enough to enter the scene together, not a completed biography.

Check their records with them. Ask each player to explain a capability, its ordinary use, one limitation, and the bonus they will add to a check. If someone cannot answer, help rewrite the capability before adding more options. A readable narrow build is a stronger teaching tool than a large unexplained package.
Prepare facts instead of a sequence

Write what exists, what people want, and what is changing. Avoid “first they persuade, then they fight, then they repair.” A player may repair immediately, persuade someone unexpected, or leave to get help. Your prepared facts should survive those choices.

For the sluice example, the gate is physically jammed, a downstream bed needs protection, workers know a passage, and the rising water threatens routes. Those facts support several solutions. If the party creates a new safe path, use it. If they persuade the Watchers, the creatures do not need to attack anyway to satisfy your outline.

Give important information through more than one source. A worker knows the passage; a painted maintenance arrow points toward it; an old map shows it. You can still hide optional secrets. The immediate problem should not stop because one die failed to reveal the only usable route.
Teach the first roll without shorthand

Describe the uncertainty before naming a practice. Show the full calculation: die, current attribute, applicable training, other modifiers, and DC. Then show the combined sheet bonus and explain that it already includes those contributions.

Use a small consequence the group can understand. A failed diagnosis might cost time and change a route. If injury or death is a real stake, establish it clearly. Do not use a first-session failure to teach that the DM can attach an unrelated punishment after the roll.

When advantage appears, explain conditions and cancel opposing stacks. One remaining stack means two dice; two means three. Select the die and add the static bonus once. A visible example is easier to remember than a paragraph of probability theory.
Introduce a round when timing matters

Use Council, Fast, Measured, and Heavy when actions meaningfully depend on or oppose each other. Explain that the round is shared. Gather coherent Main Intents and ask which need another result. Give the opposition visible behavior.

At first, keep the number of independent enemy workings small. A Watcher turns a current; a second guards a spawning bed. Their different intentions create a useful scene without requiring a hidden action list. Complexity determines track placement; output size is a different question.

Track movement and one ordinary independent Reaction Slot. A player moving 10 ft in Fast with Speed 30 has 20 ft left, not a new allowance in Measured. A reaction needs an actual trigger, opportunity, and scope. Explain these when someone proposes a response, rather than interrupting the opening scene with every exception.
End with a playable next step

Reserve a few minutes for the changed world. Who trusts the party? What remains damaged? Which consequences still apply? What do the players want next? A concise record can make the next session easy to begin.

Ask one question about comprehension and one about enjoyment. “Which rule was hard to find?” produces a different answer from “Which choice did you want more of?” Treat those answers as evidence. The published book cannot substitute for observing your particular table.

Agree any BU rewards separately from the fictional gratitude or treasure. Do not award a mandatory amount just because the scene used combat. Let the table know how advancement will work in this campaign.
A workshop in understandable rulings

The following cases are **optional example rulings**, not an extra mandatory tariff. Each shows how a DM can preserve creativity while identifying missing access, changed scope, and consequences. Use the actual circumstance at your table.
The unseen target behind a wall

A player says, “I have Far, so I hit the guard in the next room.” Ask how the actor locates that guard and how the working is delivered. Ordinary hearing may reveal an approximate sound without fixing the exact location. A granted sense can supply more information if its rule actually does so.

A projected bolt is blocked by total cover on its path. Direct manifestation avoids intervening projected-cover penalties, but still needs valid targeting and the corresponding behavior. Far does not establish either. The player can target a known spot with an appropriate area construction and accept uncertainty, move to gain sight, use a relevant sense, or propose another authored targeting method.

Say which part is missing. “You know someone spoke in the room, but your present sense does not locate their body precisely; the wall also blocks this projected path” lets the player revise the attempt. “No, your spell cannot do that” does not explain the permission problem.
A flood rather than a bowl

Mira's Water and Verb II support reshaping existing water. A bowl and a surging street are eligible subjects of different scale and pressure. Ask which portion she wants to change, where it goes, how soon, and whether the result must persist.

Offer alternatives tied to those facts: a narrow safe lane, help from workers with boards, or a slower diversion before the storm peak. An agreed cost might restrict Mira while she maintains the lane, damage an outlet, or create a later obligation. Do not convert every larger expression into fixed Vitality damage.

A larger cost does not give her Life access or guarantee rescue of every person in the water. If she wants to heal them as well, review that extra behavior explicitly. Maintaining the channel can spread pressure over time without a compulsory percentage discount.
A small character and a large sword

The base equipped-slot rule is one for an ordinary item and two for a two-handed item. Size does not automatically multiply that final requirement. The Rule of Cool can support an unusual sword with its own authored slot cost or consequence.

Discuss how the character carries, braces, and uses it. A three- or four-slot requirement can make the choice meaningful. A restriction in cramped spaces may fit another concept. Record the actual item terms; do not create a secret size formula that changes unrelated equipment.

Keep Load, Item BU, ordinary value, and equipped use separate. A sword can be expensive in the setting without a large Item BU figure. Extra slots do not increase carrying capacity. Giving an unusual item permission to work in this scene does not grant automatic reach, damage dice, or resistance.
A strong argument and a frightened person
An Influence check resolves uncertainty in an approach. It does not erase a motive or establish mind control. Ask what the speaker offers and what the listener reasonably believes.

A guard who fears punishment may accept a credible written authorization, a witness, or a plan to share responsibility. A large number alone is not the offer. If the response is secure once those facts are established, no roll is necessary. If uncertainty remains, name what success changes: a temporary passage, a private conversation, or willingness to hear evidence.

A capability that overrides agency belongs to a different construction and needs explicit behavior, recipients, resolution, limits, and consent at the table. Do not use ordinary negotiation as a covert substitute for that permission.
A moment that matters more than a formula

A player wants to leap farther than ordinary movement allows to catch a falling companion. Establish location, available movement, actual reaction opportunity, and the physical route. The table may agree extra movement with a consequence or a bounded cinematic exception.

State the exception before resolution. Perhaps the leap reaches the companion but leaves both hanging from the ledge, or spends a resource and makes retreat difficult. If the proposed consequence is unacceptable, the player can choose another response. Spending a Reaction Slot alone grants neither unlimited distance nor guaranteed rescue.
Record the reason for the ruling: unstable ledge, visible falling ally, reachable handhold, agreed exertion. This preserves consistency without turning the exceptional rescue into permanent flight.
A lasting injury without a hidden package

A character accepts “burned hands.” Ask what that does. A specific -2 to delicate Finesse checks is different from an inability to hold a tool, a reduction of Physical, or loss of an acquired permission.

Record recovery. Dressing and an agreed rest may clear a minor consequence; a severe injury can need another stated treatment. Healing Vitality does not automatically clear either unless the consequence says so. Avoid leaving a player with an undefined indefinite penalty.

Narrative description can coexist with a mechanical rule. The wrapped hands show what happened; the record explains how to play it. A later revision should be discussed, not silently broadened during an important action.
An ambiguous new primitive

A player proposes “Always succeed at hiding.” Ask what information, recipients, conditions, and resolution the rule intends. It could mean a bonus, a result floor, invisibility, erasing evidence, or overriding others' perception. Those are different effects.

Help produce a narrower first version: a specific bonus to concealment through movement under stated conditions, or an authored sense-obscuring behavior with limits. Review price and stacking afterward. Do not assume a chosen BU number makes an unreadable rule understandable.

Test normal, stretched, and outside-scope uses. If a primitive's definition supports contradictory outcomes, fix the definition before judging its cost. A clear inexpensive rule is more useful than a grand title with a large number.
Creatures from a purpose to a record

A creature begins with an encounter use, not a difficulty label. Ask what it wants, how it changes the scene, what players can perceive, and what can stop the confrontation without killing it. Then build the actual permissions supporting that behavior.

The records here are original **authored examples** using the current creature foundation and reference anchors. Example custom prices require table review. They are not new compulsory catalogue entries. Unspent budget is shown honestly; it grants no hidden ability.
The foundation arithmetic

Choose a positive base budget B. Rank is sqrt(B/25). Base attribute points are ceil(3 × rank); PB is 1 + ceil(rank); baseline maximum Vitality is max(1, ceil(B/2)). These are creature baselines, not the character's 10-point allocation and level-based Vitality formula.

Allocate nonnegative base attribute points and choose the proficient attribute. Read the full current parent attribute for each practice check, then its actual training and modifiers. Digital practice-allocation slices satisfy the allocation ledger; a small slice is not a second reduced check modifier.

At B 50, rank is not rounded to 1 before the other formulas. ceil(3 × sqrt(2)) is 5 and 1 + ceil(sqrt(2)) is 3. Round at the specified stage. If an explicit agreed Vitality override or active primitive changes the result, record it separately.
Canal Watcher: a small guardian

Use the complete 25-BU Canal Watcher record in Worked records. Its 20 spent BU supports Verb II, Water I, Near, and d8. It has five remaining, no equipment, no mirror credit, and no unlisted action economy. Physical 2, Mental 0, Magical 1; Magical proficient; PB 2; DC 8; maximum Vitality 13.

Its value in a scene comes from turning a current near a spawning bed. Telegraph that concern before it attacks. Give it a path to negotiation: a credible diversion preserving the bed. Its location near useful water supports its capabilities; a dry bank changes its opportunities.

One Watcher can warn and manipulate a small channel. Two can guard different objectives, disagree about people, or cooperate. Do not treat quantity as an automatic license to apply the same consequence to every character. Each creature has its own intent, position, state, and reaction availability.
Sluice Warden: a sturdier protector

**Purpose.** A constructed keeper braces damaged waterworks and prevents sudden releases. It is patient when shown a safe repair plan and forceful when someone tears a control away. Its visible tell is a rising arm pressed against the gate brace.

Base budget 100; rank 2; six base attribute points allocated Physical 3, Mental 1, Magical 2. Magical is proficient; baseline PB 3 and Vitality 50. One acquired Physical increment changes current Physical to 4. Magical-selected DC is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.

rows: Reach up to 30 ft with valid targeting
Basic spatial/group arrangements within actual access
Halve Physical damage, rounded up, while both feet and one hand brace the fixed sluice
Add +1 Physical at this accepted scope
Add PB to its Physical save

blocks.text: Braced Resistance is an authored conditional defense with a proposed 8-BU price. It affects covered Physical damage, not every source, every consequence, or allies. Breaking the brace removes its qualification; merely naming it a Warden does not grant permanent armor.

**Derived checks and saves.** Physical practices +4; Mental practices +1; Magical practices +5. Saves Physical +7, Mental +1, Magical +5. Current Physical affects carrying capacity but does not change the base allocation ledger. Large size gives walking 40 ft, ordinary swim/climb 20 ft, six equipment slots, and capacity 80 + 5 × 4 = 100 Load.

**Guiding Wall.** Use Water, Verb II, Near, and Structure II to organize a located band of existing water into a temporary directed obstruction. State shape, affected route, opposition, and continuation. The normal example is a short lane beside the gate, maintained while braced. It does not automatically immobilize every creature or negate attacks; resolve actual crossings and interference.

**Pressure Strike.** Project existing water along a path within 30 ft. Attack +5 against the target's DC; normal hit expression 1d8 Magical Water. Cover applies to the projected path. Larger output or additional targets needs appraisal, not an automatic extra Main Intent.

**Equipment.** A Medium fixed-hook brace has Item BU 4, Load 2, and two final equipped slots. Its authored rule gives +2 to Prowess checks to hold a gate while the hook is firmly anchored; it affects that check, not Physical. Such qualifying Prowess is +6. Item BU stays separate from the 52 creature BU. Unequipping it removes the conditional equipment contribution and frees its slots, but its carried Load remains.

**Counter-approaches.** Show the brace and control route. A player can negotiate a safer flow, unanchor the hook, or draw the Warden away from the fixed sluice. A strong defense becomes an observable choice rather than a concealed statistic.
Bellhouse Custodian: an asymmetric solo

**Purpose.** The Custodian guards a mechanism that records binding promises. It wants the bells in their proper order and will pursue someone who removes a marked counterweight. Its tell is a slow raising of two separate hammer arms: one protects the mechanism, one threatens the route.

Base budget 225; rank 3; nine base attribute points allocated Physical 4, Mental 2, Magical 3. Magical proficient, PB 4, Vitality 113. Magical-selected DC 12. Large walking 40 ft and swim/climb 20 ft; capacity 100 Load; six slots. Physical practices +4, Mental +2, Magical +7; saves Physical +4, Mental +2, Magical +7.

rows: Halve Physical Metal damage, rounded up; no other source/domain defense
One additional independent Reaction Slot per round, same ordinary trigger/scope limits
Explicit authored grants; no mirror credit

blocks.text: The conditional scope and 8/12-BU custom prices are example authoring choices. The large remaining budget is not converted into automatic damage, extra phases, or secret abilities. Its base foundation already differs greatly from a low-budget creature. You can develop the record further through real acquisitions when the campaign needs that, rather than spending numbers merely to fill a bar.

**Hammer Sweep.** Manipulate existing metal within 60 ft through an actual supported path. Normal single-target attack +7, 1d10 Magical Metal on a hit. A line affecting several recipients is a different declared expression supported by Structure II and appraised for scale, targeting, and consequences; the normal attack line does not silently contain it.

**Hold the Counterweight.** Redirect a located metal counterweight to hold the central lift. Continuing the example binds one hammer arm to that task. Releasing it changes the lift's position as agreed. It is a restrictive upkeep requirement, not a compulsory Vitality payment.

**Second Response.** Two slots are available at Council because the explicit acquisition says so. Each response still needs a perceived valid trigger, immediate eligible scope, and remaining movement or other actual access. A boss title, Large size, or 225 base BU would not provide these slots without the authored grant. The Custodian retains one coherent Main Intent by default.

**Practical solo design.** Threaten an objective as well as Vitality. The party may split between restoring bell order, keeping the lift open, and negotiating the promise's meaning. Tell them what the arms are doing. Let interference change opportunities. A second response makes the creature more responsive, not immune to every plan.
Review before running

Read each creature's definition aloud in the voice of a new DM. Can you identify its attack bonus, damage source/domain, sense, path, reaction capacity, and ending conditions? If not, repair the record before it appears in a tense scene.

Test a favorable situation, a counter-approach, and a changed environment. The Watcher loses useful water; the Warden loses its brace; the Custodian must protect a lift while negotiating. Such tests reveal dependencies that a total BU comparison cannot.

Keep build and appraisal ledgers separate. Two Wardens are 200 enemy creature BU plus 8 Item BU, not 104 creature BU because each spends 52, and not 208 creature BU with equipment counted again. Quantities create independent creatures; they do not merge their Vitality into one shared bar unless a deliberately authored exception says so.
Run an encounter through its whole life

Preparation, active play, and aftermath need different records. A compact preparation can become a useful run sheet without carrying every paragraph into every round. Keep definitions accessible, but track only the state that is changing now.
Prepare the choices

Write the objective, opening situation, visible pressure, and plausible alternatives. Put distances, barriers, resources, and sensory conditions where you can find them. A roster alone is not an encounter: it does not say why people are present or what a good outcome might be.

Record Party BU and Party Item BU separately, with party size if known. Manual totals are sufficient. Linked character totals can help, but access to a sheet is not editing permission. In the digital workflow, calculated totals replace manual values only when the GM chooses to apply them; later changes should be refreshed intentionally.

Record each template's chosen base budget, exact version, Item BU, and quantity. A pinned definition makes the preparation reproducible. Updating a version can change the creature; review that change rather than assuming the same name means the same mechanics.
Use comparisons as facts

Enemy count compared with party size tells you how many independent positions and responses may matter. A budget concentrated in one creature tells you that one loss or control effect can change the scene sharply. Several support creatures can create different pressures from a single opponent with the same total.

For a party of three default starting characters, Party BU is 75 before equipment. Two Watchers contribute 50 creature BU and zero Item BU. If party equipment is 8 Item BU, combined party is 83 and enemy is 50. Difference is -33; ratio is 50/83. This arithmetic says nothing automatic about safety. A flood, rescue duty, surprise treatment, or difficult targeting can dominate the actual scene.

Do not label this “easy” solely from the ratio. Describe control, area effects, support, burst, terrain, information, and alternative objectives. Comparable totals are not a promise of comparable difficulty.
Start with independent state

Each creature needs its own current Vitality, position, consequences, reaction availability, and maintained work. Name repetitions clearly. Watcher 1 may negotiate while Watcher 2 remains angry; sharing a definition does not make their decisions or injuries identical.

In the platform, starting a run creates independent private play copies from the prepared pins. Starting another run creates fresh copies and preserves the earlier run. Previewing or adding a template does not create a creature immediately. Paper play can achieve the same separation with one short state line per creature.
Council is a coordination point

Present the changed battlefield. Resolve agreed continuing requirements, reset ordinary independent reactions, and ask for coherent Main Intents. Record track placement and dependencies. Avoid carrying last round's resolved marker as a permanent status.

You can speak for several enemies without hiding their observable plans. “The Warden braces the gate while the Watcher turns toward the eastern channel” provides usable information. What the characters cannot perceive can remain uncertain, but all opposition should not become a private sequence of surprises.
Resolve the changed scene

When intents intersect, decide whether the question is timing, directly opposed effort, hitting, or resisting. Use the matching procedure. Do not add a clash and a contest and an attack and a save to the same moment merely because all four exist.

A failed timing roll changes who acts first; it does not universally delete the loser's intent. A disrupted route can require a pivot. A reaction pauses its triggering event, resolves a valid response, then resumes from the new facts. Positions and movement used stay continuous across tracks.

Advancing the phase is an organizational action. It does not automatically damage creatures, expire consequences, heal characters, or resolve an upkeep requirement. Apply actual rules and endings deliberately. Digital state controls should support that work rather than invent it.
End without erasing history

Mark the immediate result: objective achieved, retreat, negotiated agreement, changed control, or unresolved danger. Ending the encounter does not delete playable copies or erase consequences. A creature can remain injured; a promise can remain binding; a damaged place can matter next session.

Record who witnessed the result and which relationships changed. Ask players what they want to follow. Archive the run when useful. A future replay or new run starts its own state, not a retroactive rewrite of this encounter.
Adventure: the gate that will not open

**Original teaching adventure.** A canal settlement faces rising water and a jammed sluice. Two guardians fear for a downstream spawning bed. Workers need safe access to the mechanism. This adventure teaches a visible problem, ordinary tools, supernatural access, negotiation, shared timing, and consequences that can be restrictive or environmental.

**Preparation.** Use two 25-BU Canal Watchers from Worked records, no equipment, 50 total enemy creature BU. This is a starting roster, not a difficulty guarantee. A party such as the three workshop characters has 75 Party BU; record its actual equipment separately. Reduce or omit opposition if your group's needs suggest it. The guardians do not attack simply because the record contains an attack.
Opening and immediate facts

Read or paraphrase: “Brown water climbs the gauge beside the sluice. Workers lean against a rope that shudders with each surge. Across the channel, a small river spirit points urgently toward reeds below the gate. Someone calls from a maintenance door: the upper wheel is jammed.”

Give visible distances from the map. The central gate is 30 ft from the western landing. The east bank is another 30 ft beyond it. A lower maintenance route runs 40 ft beneath the western wall. The spawning bed lies downstream, outside the immediate gate platform. The schematic labels measured routes; room footprints and line lengths are not to scale. There is no imported diagonal-movement rule.

The water is rising because a snapped timber blocks the wheel, not because someone casts a hidden spell. The guardians are protecting eggs and young river life. Workers want to prevent a release into the houses. All three concerns can coexist in a successful plan.
People with understandable motives

**Ressa, repair worker.** Wants workers safe and the gate under control. Knows the passage and how the manual wheel should move. Offers tools and directions freely to people helping. Fears an uncontrolled release because her family lives downstream. She is not a quest dispenser waiting for an Influence roll to reveal obvious facts.

**Senn, boat runner.** Wants a boat unloaded before the quay floods. Has strong rope and a small flat-bottomed boat. Can help ferry people or haul material, but needs someone to secure the mooring. A fair plan can recruit that help without a supernatural compulsion.

**The two Watchers.** One points toward the bed; the other watches the gate. They can communicate through gesture and ordinary conversation at this table. Their Water capabilities do not grant mind reading. They believe people will open the gate without considering the downstream life. Showing a credible protected flow addresses their actual objection.
Area A: the western landing

A solid lower post can anchor rope. Spare boards, a hook, and a marked maintenance arrow are available. Give these facts immediately when inspected. The post can support a rescue line; it is not infinitely strong. Agree demanding loads or sudden pressure with the actual circumstances.

The landing becomes less safe if the water continues to rise. Telegraph the change: water covers the lowest step, then the rope strains against its angle. Do not advance a hidden countdown every time a player asks a question. Use fictional time and the table's agreed urgency.

A player can recruit workers, examine the jam, or establish a line toward the wheel. Ordinary tools remain useful. A Near working from the landing can reach the gate at 30 ft if the actor can locate its eligible target; it cannot reach every point beyond it automatically.
Area B: the wheel platform

A snapped beam is caught between wheel and brace. It is visible from a close safe angle. A Reason or Knowledge check can resolve diagnosis under pressure if uncertainty matters. If someone has secure access and enough time, simply explain the jam.

Removing the beam without controlling the release risks a sudden flow. Establish that before commitment. Torren might hold the wheel with tools; Mira might redirect a narrow portion of water; Ilex might coordinate workers. Their chosen sequence affects complexity and track placement. The DM does not require one fixed “repair capability.”

A Watcher can move toward the platform to prevent an uncontrolled opening. Telegraph its intent. If timing matters, resolve the actual clash. If two actors struggle over the wheel, resolve the contest. Use the question that exists, rather than forcing both procedures onto every interaction.
Area C: the maintenance passage

The lower passage is wet, narrow, and partly blocked by debris. An arrow and Ressa's information reveal it. A printed map on the workshop wall provides a third source. No single failed search prevents discovering every alternative.

The route reaches the underside of the wheel. It can support a careful removal while someone controls the upper mechanism. Water level and tools matter. The party may prefer this route because it avoids direct confrontation on the platform; it introduces a different exposure and rescue problem.

If someone slips, locate them and explain the actual danger. A nearby catch can use an eligible reaction. A remote rescue requires relevant access and reach. Stabilization, healing, and escape remain separate questions if a character collapses.
Area D: the spawning bed

The reeds visibly shelter small river life. A Watcher points to them before using violence. Characters who investigate learn why the guardians resist. A credible protected flow can turn opposition into cooperation.

The bed is not a mandatory sacrifice. Players can use boards, a temporary diversion, a slower gate opening, or another plan. An extraordinary attempt must still have its eligible subject and behavior. Water shaping supports a flow plan; it does not automatically heal the eggs, rewrite the guardians' agency, or repair every structure.
Pressure and possible escalation

Choose changes from the visible situation. The lower step floods. The wheel tilts. A mooring loosens. A worker calls that a storehouse is taking water. Give warning and a usable response before a route disappears when the fiction allows it.

Do not attach a fixed number of rounds to the whole adventure unless your table intentionally agrees a timed treatment. Negotiation might resolve before a combat round begins. A secure repair can take minutes. A sudden slip can require the shared rhythm immediately.

If the group refuses the problem, portray a plausible aftermath. Workers evacuate, the guardians protect what they can, and the canal route may close. Their later adventures begin from that result. The world changes without punishing players simply for choosing another goal.
Three plausible resolutions

**Cooperative diversion.** The party explains a safe downstream route, recruits workers, and controls the release. The Watchers help instead of attacking. Costs can be sustained attention, damaged boards, or a repair obligation. Celebrate the actual plan rather than requiring a fight for completion.

**Forced opening.** The party drives off the Watchers and removes the beam. If they do not protect downstream life or houses, apply those established consequences. Defeating the guardians does not automatically solve the hydraulic problem. Their independent states and choices continue until the threat ends or they retreat.

**Evacuation and delayed repair.** The party secures people and accepts temporary closure. The immediate threat to life ends, but boats and supplies cannot pass. The group may need materials or specialist help next session. This is a different success, not a failed version of your preferred solution.
Aftermath and rewards

Record saved people, damaged places, guardians' attitudes, equipment use, current Vitality, and remaining consequences. Agree recovery from the actual shelter and time available. A night spent repairing in the rain is not automatically a full long rest.

If this completes a significant campaign objective, discuss advancement according to your campaign agreement. No universal BU award is attached to two defeated Watchers. Ressa's gratitude, a new route, and a promise of passage are fictional results whether or not the ledger changes.

Possible next questions: Who installed the brittle beam? Why has the upstream flow changed? What old channel became visible? Use a question the players cared about. The adventure has taught how to respond to a situation, not how to follow one mandatory plot.
Adventure: the bellhouse of borrowed names

**Original teaching adventure.** A hilltop bellhouse stores public promises in metal counterweights. An old agreement now appears to bind the wrong families. The Custodian refuses to release the central lift while its records conflict. The party must establish what changed, protect people using the lift, and choose what to do with the agreement.

This is a situation about evidence, obligation, and an asymmetric guardian. It can end through restoration, negotiation, changed terms, or force. The adventure does not presume the promise is just because an ancient mechanism preserves it.

**Preparation.** Use the 225-BU Bellhouse Custodian from Creatures from a purpose to a record. Optional two Canal Watchers, reflavored only in story as rain-fed caretakers, add 50 creature BU without changing their Water mechanics. Total with both is 275, no Item BU. This can be a severe threat to low-budget characters. Compare your actual party, telegraph danger, and offer meaningful noncombat routes; do not claim the example is balanced by its page count.
Opening and what is wrong

Read or paraphrase: “A bell sounds once, then stops halfway through its answering note. The lift hangs above the lower landing. On the hill, bronze arms brace two different counterweights. A keeper holds a cracked metal plate: the names stamped on it do not match the charter.”

The record was not maliciously altered by a hidden mastermind. Years of repair replaced one counterweight with an old spare whose binding marks belonged to another agreement. A hurried keeper failed to check the replacement. You can choose a different cause for your campaign, but establish it before clues depend on it.

The central question is not “win the boss fight.” It is what the party will do with conflicting evidence and a mechanism that acts on the marked metal. People below need a safe route; the keeper needs an understandable resolution; the Custodian needs a credible account of the bells' order.
Area E: the lower landing

The landing gives sight of the lift, 30 ft above. A stair ascends 50 ft along the outer wall to a gallery. A service path leads around the hill, longer but sheltered. The schematic identifies these alternatives and labels measured route distances. Read those labels instead of measuring the drawing.

Ordinary ladders, ropes, and workers can support a rescue. Flight or mobility grants change the route only within their actual rules. A single character reaching the lift does not automatically transport everyone. Locate passengers and explain who needs help before resolving a rescue.

The lift remains held while the Custodian maintains Hold the Counterweight. A loss of that requirement changes its state at the agreed instant. Give characters visible information about the braced arm and actual supports; do not hide a falling-lift consequence behind an innocent control button.
Area F: the archive room

There are three useful sources: the paper charter, a maintenance ledger, and the keeper's account. The charter lists the original parties. The ledger records the replacement. The keeper saw the old spare taken from storage. Each offers a route toward the mistake.

Inspection can reveal obvious differences. A Knowledge or Reason check can resolve reading a damaged entry under pressure. Ilex's Paper access can stabilize the physical sheet at Touch; it does not create missing words or prove truth automatically. Ordinary careful copying can also preserve the record.

Optional discoveries include an earlier dispute, an unfulfilled repair promise, or evidence that the original agreement unfairly burdened one group. These add decisions. They are not necessary to discover the mechanical replacement error.
Area G: the bell gallery

Three bells face different paths. Their visible marks correspond to the charter's three witness places. A worker can explain the ordinary order. The Custodian compares actual ringing and metal marks; it does not read every person's thoughts.

Players can show the mismatch, restore the old counterweight, propose a temporary suspension with an accepted obligation, or ask whose authority can change the agreement. Decide the Custodian's response from its purpose and the evidence. An Influence check may resolve uncertainty about a credible proposal, but it does not rewrite the mechanism's metal by itself.

If someone removes a counterweight without support, the Custodian responds. Telegraph which arm moves and whether the lift is threatened. Its two Reaction Slots are explicitly authored; they are not an automatic privilege of every solo creature. It has one coherent Main Intent by default.
Area H: the counterweight chamber

The chamber contains the substituted weight, the old damaged original, and tools. Existing Metal I and Verb II can support reshaping or redirecting eligible metal, but deleting a social obligation or changing a person's identity is not simply more metal manipulation.

A physical repair can restore the original mechanism while leaving the moral question unresolved. A table might agree a bounded exceptional working to transfer a mark with consequences; state its actual scope.
